THE TWO SNAILS. She was a plump little English snail, He was of French extraction; The Channel rolled between them, yet He loved her to distraction. He asked her, through the telephone In tones of deep emotion, If she would brave the sea for him, And cross the stormy ocean. "No, thank you, sir," she coyly said, "I love you, but no matter: I could not feel at home in France, Where snails are fried in batter." .--Litttle Folks Magazine for .September.

A BIRD OF PASSAGE. Swallow, swallow, onward winging, Leaving here an empty nest, Stop and tell me, 'mid thy singing, Fliest thon to east, to west?" "Lives there not a Heart that knoweth Where another nest may be? O'er the fields His birdie goeth, O'er the mountains, o'er the sea." "Swallow, little swallow, hearken! Ocean-paths'are deep and wide, Day by day the shadows darken— Who shall be thy help and guide?" "One is living, One is reigning Who shall lead His birdie's flight, Even though the days be waning— Lead me nearer to the light." "Swallow, swallow, stop and hear me— Very frail thou art and small; What if wings should droop and weary, What if thou ahouldst faint and fall ?" "Not a birdie sinking, shivering, Drops to earth alone and drear ; When the wings in death are quivering, Then the Lord of love is near." "Swallow, sing o'er field and city! Safe thou art by shore, by. sea; God doth wrap thee round m pity— Will He not remember me?' MARGARET HAYCRAFT.

• Some things are more valuable when they are upside down: A figure six, for instance. A teacher was illustrating the process of evaporation to a class of young scholars. "Suppose I should set a basin of water out in the school yard in the morning, and let it remain all day, what would happen?" "It would get upset," was the practical reply. "Laying out another railroad?" "Surveying for one," was the reply.—" Goin' threw my barn ?" "Don't see how we can avoid it."—" Wall, now, mister, I calkerlate I've got sornethin' tew say 'bout that. I want you to understan' that I've got somethin' tew dew besides ran- ring out tew open and slut them doors every time a train wants to go threw." The late William Barnes, the "Dorsetshire poet," used to tell of a little boy whom he found one day in a village school, and who had written the word "psalm" in his copy-book and then accidentally blotted out the initial "p" with his sleeve. His little sister at his side was in tears at the disaster, but the natural-born spelling re- former defiantly exclaimed, "What if I did scrope of en out? He didn't spell naught, and what was the good of en ?"

An Irishman, who was a dealer in a small way, and kept a little donkey and a cart, came on one occasion to a bridge where 'toll was levied, but, to his disappoint- ment, found that he had not enough money to pay. A thought struck him. He unharnessed the donkey and put it into the cart. Then getting in between the shafts himself, he pulled the cart with the donkey standing on it, to the bridge. In due course he was hailed by the toll-collector. "Hey, ma man," cried the latter, " whaur's your toll ?" Said the Irishman, "Just ax the droiver." _

SUPPRESS/NG A REEELLTON liT/TIZ A CARPET BAG.—King Leopold's life was indeed "a history in itself." He was almost ostentatiously indifferent to his position—ever impressing on his subjects that he reigned in their in- terest rather than in his own. It has been said that he could always bring them to reason by threatening to abdicate. The sagacity and tact with which he pre- vented the Catholics and the Liberals in Belgium from coming to blows, gave him great influence in Europe. But that influence was enhanced by his capacity for diplomatic intrigue, and the opportunities for exercising it which his curious family connections gave him. Though he began life as one of the obscurest of the petty Princes of Germany, he had married in succession the heiress of England and the daughter of the King of the French. By a double marriage, his children were allied to the Imperial House of Hapsburg. He was the uncle and mentor of the queen and the Prince Consort— indeed, he and Baron Stoclrmar had brought about their marriage. His position was supposed to be unassailable from the day when, on being threatened with a revolu- tion, he calmly began to pack a carpet-bag in presence of the popular leaders, who thereupon, in a paroxysm of fear, implored him not to leave the country. Yet, according to Lord Malmesbury, "the last years of his life were spent in perpetual terror of Louis Napoleon, and he was constantly alarming our Ministers and every- body on the subject." The Life and Times of Qyeen Victoria, for September. Sea EFFECTS IN HOLLANO.—Perhaps the most im- portant element, pictorially [in Holland], is the sea; for in a country mainly reclaimed from it. pierced in every direction by arms of it, whose riches are due to it, and which is washed on two sides by it, this must be so. If you paint in a church, the votive model of a ship, or tomb of a sea-warrior, is before you; if you compose a peaceful landscape, almost anywhere, the sail of a canal boat, or a seagull, will intrude itself. It was the sea as much as the Netherlands which drove the Spaniards from the land. An immense number of people get their living directly from the sea; and its many miles of coast i make it impossible to entirely omit it n any artistic effort, even though it be but in feeling the fact that it is present. It is indeed A land that rides at anchor, and is moored, Where people do not live, but go on-board. The shallow, stormy German Ocean, breaking in cease- less beauty on its white sands, is always a picture. Its waters' often mixed with sand, always in storms, nuske up in fine colour what it lacks in transparency—from pale blue to warm red in the wave-shadows, yellowish foam, and yet withal gray and harmonious. In high winds it breaks miles from the shore, when all the light in the picture seems to be in the mass of rushing, foam- ing water; then if through this comes the black hull and russet sails of a fishing boat, making for a place—cer- tain death to any other model—it is indeed a picture. The size of these boats makes them most useful; large enough to compose well, and yet their feeling and pathos not lost in too great evidence of safety. The almost daily going and coming of the fishers from the few vil- lages, the departure for the herring-fishing, with the groups of disconsolate wives and sweethearts, the rise and fall of the tide, with its ceaseless change of colour and conformation, are a never-failing source of interest. —Scribner's Magazine for August. BIBLE NAMES IN EAST LANCASEIRE.—If we look over pages of the directories of West Yorkshire and East Lancashire, and strike out the surnames, we could imagine we were consulting anciently inscribed registers of Joppa or Jericho. It would seem as if Canaan and Rossendale had got inextricably mixed. Within the limits of ten leaves we have three Pharaohs, while as many Hepzibahs are to be found on one single page. Adah and Zillah Pickles, sisters, are milliners; Jehoiada Rhodes makes saws—not Solomon's sort—and Hariph Crawshaw keeps a farm. Vashni, from somewhere in the Chronicles, is rescued from oblivion by Vashni Wil- kinson, coal merchant, who very likely goes to Barzillai Williamson, on the same page, for his joints, Barzillai being a butcher. Jachin, known to but few as situated in the Book of Kings, is in the person of Jachin Firth, a beer retailer, familiar to all his neighbours. Heber Holdsworth on one page is faced by Er Illingworth on the other. Asa and Joab are extremely popular, while Abner, Adna, Ashael, Erastus, Eunice, Benaiah, Aquila, Elihu, and Philemon enjoy a fair amount of patronage. Shadrack, Meshack, and Abednego are also represented. I have lighted upon name after name that I did not know existed in the Bible at all till I looked into the Lanca- shire and Yorkshire directories. The Bible has decided the nomenclature of the North of England. In towns like Oldham, Bolton, Ashton, and Blackburn, the clergy- man's baptismal register is but a record of Bible names. A clerical friend of mine christened twins Cain and Abel, only the other day, much against his own wishes. An- other parson on the Derbyshire border was gravely in- formed, at the proper moment, that the name of baptism WAS Rarnoth-Gilead. "Boy or girl, eh?" he asked, in a sernewhat agitated voice. The parents had opened the Bible haphazard, according to the village tradition, and selected the first name the eye fell on. A year ago a little child was christened Tellno, in a town within six miles of Manchester, at the suggestion of a cotton spinner, the father, a workman of the name of Lees, having asked his advice. "I suppose it must be a Scripture name," said his master. "Oh, yes; that's course." "Suppose you choose Tellno," said his em- ployer. "That'll do,' replied the other, who had never heard it before, and liked it the better on that account. The child is now Tellno Lees ("Lees" being the Lanca- shire way of pronouncing "Lies"), the father, too late, finding that he had been hoaxed. "Sirs," was the an- swer given to a bewildered curate, alter the usual demand to name the child. He objected, but was in- formed that it was a Scripture name, and the verse, "Sirs, what must I do to be saved ?" was triumphantly appealed to. This reminds one of the Puritan who styled his dog "Moreover," after the dog in the gospel: "More- over the dog came and licked his sores."—Curiosities of Puritan Nomenclature.

"I know what those men are doing with the telegraph wires," said young knickerbockers, as he gazed upward with his hands in his pockets. "Well, my boy, what are they doing with them ?" "Shaking the talk out of 'em." Pa AND TM CRILDREN.—A small boy, Tommy Peterby, who is one of a family of ten, was taken out in the family carriage with his mother. As they drove past a small cottage of three rooms, Mrs. Peterby remarked libw pretty it looked. "Yes, it looks very nice," said Tommy; and it wouldn't be a bit too big for our family, if it wasn't for pa and the children." A SUGGESTION.—A Dallas lady was giving her daughter instructions in etiquette, and how to acquire a husband. "If a gentleman enters the room, etiquette demands that you arise from your seat, and advance a few steps to meet him, with a bright, sunny smile." "But suppose no gentleman ever comes into the room ?" "Then, of course, you don't change your position: you remain just as you are." "My dear," said a petulant editor to his wife, who asked him a civil question, "why do you persist in dis- turbing me when you see that I am wrapped in thought ?" "Because," she replied, "I am afraid you'll take cold." "Take cold?" "Yes; when I find you are only wrapped in thought, I don't care if rt is summer time, but such covering is entirely too thin for this season." No REGARD FOR HER FEELINGE.—An Austin family has a coloured servant that, while very attentive to her duties, has never been known to give anybody a civil answer. Purely as an experiment the lady of the house bought her a new calico dress, and gave it to her, say- ing: "I am glad to have the pleasure, Matildy, of giving you this dress." "Yet mout hab had dat pleasure long ago, ef yer had had any regard fo' my feelings," was the gracious reply. Cincinnati banker's wife: "My dear, you must give little Dick a spanking, and a hard one, too." Great banker: "I havn't time. I must—" Wife: "But it won't do to overlook this fault. He stole all the money you brought home from the Sunday school collection, and then went out and pitched pennies with it." Banker: "Great Ceesar ! Lost every cent of it, I suppose?" Wife: " No ; he won a lot more that some other boy had taken from his father." Banker "Oh ! Tell him to put my money back where he got it, like an honest boy.' In a Massachusetts town some thirty years ago, when, as now, the Congregationalist parish was made up of the I exoteric "society" and the esoteric "church," the profane society, *hich votes and pays the vulgar necessary money for parish purposes, had certain liberal views which it proposed to have carried out. The indignation of the church was great, but it found no adequate ex- pression till one elderly raember rose and put it all in one bold metaphor: "It such things as these is to be done. Mr. Moderator, I think we had better go further; 1 I think we'd better rip up the bars at both eends, and let the vineyard of the Lord run rampart." REMOVING TEMYTATION.—YOUng heiress to her lover: "There is one thing that must be positively understood between us before we marry." Her ardent lover; "Name it, dearest. No matter what the conditions, I accept them in advance." Young heiress: "Under no circum- stances will I ever make a will in your favour, and you , must never even hint at such a thing." Her ardent I lover : "I do not seek you for your wealth, dearest, but why do you make such a condition?" Young heiress: "Because, my love, you are a doctor, and as you might possibly be called on to treat me, I do not want to put temptation in your way."--San Francisco Post. A LF.OEND OF BRARMAR.—According to the legend, I the district was once peopled by giants, so tall that they I could stride from hill-top to hill-top without descending into the glens, which must have greatly facilitated High- land travel. The chief pastime of these Brobdignagians was hunting wild boars, which were of commensurate size, and possessed, in addition, a most obnoxious pecu- liarity: for they were covered with long, sharp, tubular spines, in the hollow of which was so deadly a poison that if any one had the ill-luck to prick even his finger enough to draw blood, he was sure to die. The chase, then, was a perilous one; but it was rendered more easy by a want of fixity of purpose in the porcine mind. This was turned to advantage tn the following manner :—The giants took their stand on the hill-tops surrounding a boar's lair. One of them then uttered a peculiar cry, on hearing which the beast charged in the direction of the noise; but before it could reach the hunter another repeated the same cry, whereupon it turned upon him; a third then took up the note, and so on, till the boar was thoroughly wearied, and was easily knocked on the head. Now, after a time discord broke out among the giants, owing to the usual cause. One of their number had been more successful than the rest in winning the heart of an exceptionally fair giantess, and it occurred to his rivals that if they omitted to give the cry when the boar charged towards him, the damsel would have need of another suitor. The plan was tried, but to their chagrin, when they went to ascertain its success, the boar lav dead, and the young giant stood by it un- harmed. Unluckily his chief was among his enemies and was equal to the occasion, for after due compli- ments, he bade him measure the spoil. The young Titan obeyed, and measured length and breadth un- scathed; but on attempting, in consequence of a further order, to ascertain its girth, pierced his hand with a spine, and so perished. A curse, however, fell upon his treacherous brethren, and they drooped and died: all but one, who took to plundering the people, and was at last outwitted and brought to his grave by a woman's craft, with attendant circumstances that in some respects remind us of the story of Ulysses and Polyphemus.— Our Own Country. LIFE ATA FRENCH WATERINC-PLACE.—Take, for nstan ce, a typical day spent at Dieppe or Etretat. Coffee and rolls are served in your bedroom at the hotel at seven or eight o'clock, and you then rise and make a morning toilet for the beach. By half-past nine or ten the shore is crammed I with bathers and onlookers, and a sufficiently diverting spectacle is provided for those who only care to look on. Mme. la Marquise de la Vieille Roche is descending from her cabine, elaborately attired in a peignoir, a much- trimmed bathing costume, an oilskin cap, a straw hat, shoes, brace lets, and sometimes anklets. Or Monsieur, Madame, and Bbd are all proceeding in Indian file down the planks to the sea ; Monsier boldly heading the little procession, Madame following, and Bebe bringing up a shivering rear. The morning bathe over, we are all ready for the excellent dliellner a la fourchette which all French hotels provide, and after that we have the whole day to walk and drive, to read novels on the casino terrace, go out fishing, or, if we have a sand shore, to eally forth and catch shrimps. This species a "sport" is much affected on the Normandy coast, and I have seen great ladies from the Faubourg St. Germain wandering over the sands, clad only in a bathing- costume, a short checked tweed jacket, a small hat trimmed with flowers and covered with an ample gauze veil, and a shrimping-net. From seven to eight you dine, and then wend your way to the casino, where an evening's amusement is always provided in the shape of a concert, a play, or a dance. By half-past eleven you are in bed. In addition, at the larger towns, like Dieppe and Trouville, there is afways a race-week, during which feminine society runs riot in the matter of gorgeous attire. Dieppe—at least, during the month of August— is perhaps the liveliest of all French watering-places, and receives annually a large contingent of English people. The best hotels are extremely expensive, and those people who do not care to d'ress three or four times a day will do wisely to stay away—at any, rate, during the race-week, when the whole of la haute gomme, as well as all those leaders of Parisian society who affect to be specially "smart," are always to be found there. Lord Salisbury's villa, the Chalet Cecil, is near Dieppe, and the Premier and his family are always installed there during the early weeks of autumn.—The "Lady's World" for September. "Hyacinth !" "You know," the girl continued, not seeming to heed him, and now her colour rose, her eyes wavered for a second, "that in asking me to acquiesce in that lie you are yielding all you claimed two days ago." She saw his right hand clench like a vice as it hung by his side; the handsome head bowed before her. He spoke low and steadily. "I yielded that claim when you came here to-night --the saviour of my life—casting yourself on my honour." " rsaid ' all ' you claimed," said Hyacinth. Lorraine looked up, a sudden flash in his dark eyes —but perhaps he dared not trust the wild hope that for a second made his brain dizzy, for he sternly mas- tered himself, and said—though now he spoke with more effort—" All claim I yield, but not—hot the belief that—" He faltered and turned aside. One step, and Hyacinth's white hand was on his arm. "That I,' she said, her head drooping, her voice seareely above a whisper, "was unjust to yon then; no, no, I know that is not what you would' have said; but it is true; only it was because 1, did not know my own heart—did not understand " She struggled for self-command—the flashed face sank lower; bue', Lorraine waited for no more; his arms were round her 't once again, folding the trembling form to his breast ; ' his lips met hers in a long, long kiss—no word for many moments of rapture too deep for speech, and then only a broken, passionate whisper—" My darling —my wife—my own, my own!" And presently, still clinging to him, the girl lifted earnest, wistful eyes to and pleaded softly—" You will forgive me—my cruel words to you have stabbed me so keenly. 1 knew--when I was alone—that you were right when you said I had given you mope than I myself dreamed of; but I should have known it sooner, and sinned you pain !" " Hush ! hush! sweetheart; it is I, not you, who .1 must kneel as a supplicant, for I have indeed sinned-- and sinned deeply—through many yleare • and I have wronged yon too, Hyacinth—aye, your -love may for- give—did not four own dear lips tell me that if you loved me you could forgive all—trust all ?—yet my lips must still ask the boon.* "Not if the asking wounds ?" said Hyacinth. " My soul! is all blotted out—all?—all the evil past ----all word, and look, and deed that gave you just ranee for resentment even that lust act when I took you in my arms and kissed your lips, and dared to claim you. as my 'own?" Hyacinth did not answer, ,hiding her face, And Lor- raine drew a quick breath of pain; his own self reproach deceived him and made him misunderstand her; but the girl lifted her head, speaking passionately—" Au no—,not that—you misread me! I know you were- wrong in ,that—but—but—" the curly) head went down again, and the sweet voice sank quite to a whisper— could not be angry—though indeed I tried to be !" "Oh, Hyacinth!" mortal man could not forbear a smile then, "my winsome love, with a child's soul and a woman's heart,--Was I not right when I said that you were not to be won by conventional wooing ?" "Yes," said she, humbly, but smiling too, "and I don't know how I was so foolish. I ought to have known that almost from the—l mean for a long time— you were to me what no ode- else had been or ever cohld be." , "First thoughts are best, sweetheart," said Lorraine, wickedly. "Almost from the beginning"—.that is thrue for you,' isn't it? and for that reason I like it better. But you were not foolish, Hyacinth, only— what more than half won my heart—a child in many things—pure as the sky, and bright as thh sun- shine.' He Wised her tenderly; then face and manner changed. He relaxed his clasp, and seemed as if he would have put her from him. The pain was hers now; the sensative spirit was wounded instantly—not by him, but for him. She looked up with a quick, half wondering question in her eyes, and her hand clung to his. "Hyacinth;'" he said, not immediately answering the mute appeal; "/ must he quite true with- you. There must be nothing hidden. When you thought over what passed between us two days ago, did you think I spoke in the mere hurry of passion when I said no human being should stand between us—that you should be mine, though you had denied me your love ?" "No ; I knew yoll meant it.'' "Meant it to the uttermost ? " "To the uttermost,' said the girl, steadily. 'el knew you would not give me up—l cannot be as good as you think I am," she said, naively, resting her head against him, and instinctively he drew her close again; "or I should have condemned you for that, and—l did not." "Your own strong will, sweetheart, rings so much in harmony with Mine. Go on. "I thought," the girl continued, "that you would try to persuade me to elope with you; and if I would' not, and my mother would still not give me to you, then, if you knew I loved 'you, you would carry me off, and: trust that you could make me forgive you." '"Ab, true heart of woman! • You never so wronged me as to believe I could hold you prisoner till fear of the world's censure made you obedient to my will,- Hyacinth, you judged me justly. I made no denial and plead no excuse; but I would not have been your gaoler one hour. If despite year love for me and mime,

"I knew it, I knew it, said the girl, wincing Tinder his words—he neeeled no defence to her !—but a quick shadow of dread, too, crossed the young face, and he divined what brought the shadow, and said gently— " You think your mother will still deny you to me.. Hyacinth?' "She said that if even I loved you she wonld not yield her consent; she does not trust you. She thinks you could not make me happy." "I thin' ,he will yield, nyacinth, but if not—you know lau ii your hands now—ikyou will not disobey her, I am hound hand and foot; the life you have saved is yours." , "Yes, yes—mine—because you love me—not be- cause I saved it!" said the girl, clinging to him in a kind of terror. "Oh, we must not be parted! I could not live without you All shadow of doubt passed from Vincent Lorraine's ,heart, as with a deep, soft smile in his dark eyes he pressed his lips 6) his betrothed's white brow; she was his own, come what may; her love gave full answer to the fearless aterAnce of, his—that no human being ghn....::ijrte6rween -He drew her pre,ssntlftriheitnassitting dovvii briver questioned_her as to her discovery of the pro- kosed invasion of 'tile -castle. Then she told ;him of her' f.LuSkicfm,),ll, how she had watched, how Regan's words anT 'confh:in bad quickened her suspicions, how she had gone to Grady's •farm for the purpose of discovering all she could, and how she there be- came aware that there was to be a rendezvous at the farm. i "And you know," she said, with a su&lei mem laugh, " had yielded to your precious proposiiia about my presence here, it would have been no good, for I left my hat behind the corn stacks; it was white, And might have betrayed me, or flown off while k was running." "By heaven!" said Lorraine, laughing as merrily as she did, "that is genuivie comedy in the midst of some- thing very like tragedy. I thought it had flown off— that is, when I thought about it at all. Certainly that would have decided the question if nothing else had. And now, sweetheart, it's just half-past three, and almost daylight, and it has been raining heavily, by the way, for the last hour, and we have not noticed it. Will you not lie down for a little and try to rest! I shall simply reconnoitre and watch 'the enemy.' I will not fire a shot till I see what their tactics are. Besides they will probably be in hiding at present, waiting for me.'

"I should iiot sleep," said Hyacinth, "but I will do anything yon wish." "As you have always done, Lorraine could not re- sist saying, "despite the haughty looks and snubs you often gave me; and for which, faith, I loved you the better. Then, for a time, my darling, farewell. How little I dreamed, Hyacinth, when I left you, vowing to see you again though the heavens should fall, how we should meet In truth—not by my haughty will but by your noble devotion./' tt

div.head: PRESCOT.
div.p: PRESCOT.

WESLEYAN METHODIST CHAMBL.-011liktair two les- mons were preached at this chapel by the Rev, Thomas Jackson, one of the newly-appointed ministers to this cir- cuit who is about to reside and labour in Prescot, in con- nection with the above society. The service in the morn- ing was held at 10-30, and in the evening at six:o'clock. Collections were made at the close of each service in aid of the trust funds, and tows: defraying the cost of the con- templated enlargement and furnishing of the vestry and class rooms.

BREACH or THE PEACE.—At the Prescot Petty Sessions, on Tuesday, Joseph Woodward and Hannah Gore were summoned on a charge of committing a breach of the peace in Chapel street, Prescot, on the 28th August. Woodward was ordered to be bound over for his good behaviour ; and the summons against Mrs. Gore was diemissed.—James Orford, a painter, and Mary Dowd were charged with a similar offence at Prescot on the 20th ult. Both defendants were ordered to lek boind over to keep the peace. CONGREGATIONAL SUNDAE Satoor...—On Monday, the scholars in the class conducted by Mr. Dickinson at the above school made the first of their annual summer excur- sion. The party, accompanied by Mrs. Dickinson, pro- ceeded from Prescot by the 8-36 traio. They arrived t 4 Liverpool shortly after nine o'clock, and after spending some hours in visitinig Whitely's waxwork exhibition and the public museum, they proceeded to New Brighton, where tbe rest of the day was spent in visiting the chief places of attraction, and promenading along the shore. Tne party arrived home at eight o'clock, thoroughly pleased with the &We outing. ASSAULTING A WITNESS.—MAGISTERIAL CAUTION.—Be- fore Messrs F. W. Earle and W. L. Evans and Lieutenant- Colonel W. W. Pilkington, at the Prescot Petty Sessions on Tuesday, John Jones, a rough-looking man residing in Pree- cot, was charged under a warrant with assaulting an aged man named Richard Smith.—The prosecutor stated that on Saturday night he was going down "the Palk" when be met the prisoner, who mine up to him, seized him by the collar and said, "you old —, you gave me six months once." He replied that he did net, as if he (the prisoner) had been quiet he would have got nothing. The prisoner then seized and refused to let him go, but when evitness got away the prisoner came after him and kicked him on the ankle. In renter to Superiatendent Barker, prosecutor added that in 1884 he was a witness for the eolice in a charge of stabbing against the prisoner, and prisoner was sentenced to six months imprisonment. The prisoner since coming out of prison had threatened him re- peatedlye—Prisoner denied having threatened the prose- cutor, and said be did not kick him. He called two women, Mary and Elizebeth Donnelly, as witnesses.— Superintendent Barker stated that the prisoner had been fifteen times previously convicted, once for stabbing. On that occasion the prosecutor was the only witness for the police,, and the prisoner had evidently owed him a grudge since then.—The Bench stated that they could not call it a had assault, but there was a circumstance about it, that be threatened the man because he once appeared as a wit- ness against him. He would be fined 20s and costs, or one month's imprisonment. They advised the prisoner not to have anything to do with threatening witnesses after ap- pearing against him or anyone else. It was a dangerous game to play.

On Saturday, the employes of the London and North western Railway Works at etewn started on their Annual excursion. Eight special heavily-laden trains left with the men a,nd their families, four for Blackpool and four for Ruston, whilst others of the employs went away by ordinary trains to North Wales and other places.

! A SRIP liumirmn ar'Sf4A. —The captain and crew of the. barque East Lomond were larded at Plymouth on Sun- day, their vessel having been burnt at sea. She was bound from Grangemouth to Buenos Ayres with coals. but was found to be on fire shortly after leaving Eng- land. Water was continually poured on the cargo, but : unavailingly, and shortly after the ship was abandoned, she was in flames from stem to stern. The crew, pulled ' -about for 22 hours, and eventually arrived at Teneriffe,

I Mr. W. Jarrett, who was 'fortunate 'enough to escape, , says: I occupied a front seat in 'the Stalls. Between the second and fourth acts ,I left the theatre. 'Soon after I returned I saw the. drop scene fall•almost on Mr. Gra- ham's head ail* was speaking his lines. He finished what he had to say after•the curtain hatineassed his face, and I remarked to a friend, What .a strange thing. I never saw that occur before." Atli* same moment the curtain came forward with a great pelf anti seemed to graze my forehead. I saw at the sides mettiorand flame, arid heard a crackling. Realising abonce the terri tele,nature of the hicident I rushed for 'the door, and was over the stairs in a moment When I reached the passage on a level with the dress circle I new there was -a frightful rush for the front exit, and I turned into a • passage on the right, whieb I knew led to the special escape doors in New North-road. I fell in going over the stairs, and reached the street exhausted. Just aril reached the big doors they were thrown back, but by whom 'I cannot say. The scene in the elnerways and on the outside balconies, which were crannied with men andewomen— mostly; women—piteouslyncalling for 'rescue, and with flames near enough to bunt and scorch theinewas simply beartrending. , The general 'opinion is tiaat an iron curtaimin working order, and dropped as .quiekly as the scene was lowered, would have confined the frre to the stage and prevented the stampede and saved fife. It has transpired that there were about 200 persaias in the gallery, and tim ma. jority of the killed were there, the remainder' being occupants of the dress and oppereircles. As far as eau be ascertained all the pittites and stall occupants escaped. Colonel Fremantle, commanding the troops of she district, was present in the dress circle, and with several ladies escaped witle ease through .the front hall by the cloakrooms. The police behaved splendidly, under Captain Showers; and 150 men elf the lith Regiment ren- dered, with their engine and otherappliances, invaluable assistance. They. were direeted by Colonel Fremantle, Noble acts of rescue by civilians were numerous, and called forth the highest praise. Mr. Buckstone, the stage manager, who has lost Isis all and was 'utterly prostrated with grief, states that he was ire the dress circle when the Curtain pulfeel out, and iminediately ran along the left passage leading to the stage and shut down the iron door, only allowing three ladies to pass into the auditorium, as flames were by that time rushing from the stage up the passage, and cutting off the escape from the stalls. He told the players at,ttte mune moment to rush off by the big doer on the ether side of the stage. 'Then he ran back along the same passage, and gritting into the entrance hall leading to the , dress circle and stills, he threw out the theatre hose and I turned on the water, thus doing his best. Mr. Buckstoue ' adds that the whole theatre seemed to be in flames in ten seconds. Among the killed is a girl named Millen and 'Mrs. Miller, the girl's mother, states that she has also lost two brothers in the fire. ehe telegraphed to her son Miller, on beard the Impregnable, Devonport--" Comae at once; your wife is missing';" so that no less than four are dead belongibg to this one family alone. Considering that there were several bodies left at the top of the at air- case and in the gallery when the flames reached there and prevented further recovery the actual number of dead is probably over 1250. Nothing but the four walk of the theatre are standing, and some of them are in a dangerous condition. 'rho facilities for clearing from the pindress circle, and atalls must be considered as somewhat satisfactory under the circumstances, but it was the poor gallery people who suffered from the effects of blocks, smoke. ADC., and fell each an easy prey to the fiery fiend. A good many people from this part of the house and the dress circle might have been spared hid they not, as unfortunately Is too often the case, lost their presence of mind and rushed to windows and roof instead of the doors. As some poor souls were being dragged through the windows, the lurid flames playing within showed to what an infernal furnace the interior of one of the prettiest theatres in the country bad been reduced. The shrieks of those endeavouring to escape in the. way described were heartrending, and -when it is considered that it was by this time known to the crowd that a large number of people were perish- ing inside, the tension was simply fearful. With promp- titude really commendable the fire escape from the Guildhall was run up, and ladders were also erected against the windows, and many. brave rescues were effected in this way. The fire engines were also quickly on the spot, but so far as saving the theatre was con- cerned their efforts were futile, as the building burnt, as It was.expressed in the crowd, like a piece of paper. Poor distracted people mourning the less .of relatives were wandering about the streets; arid at the hospital the scene was also a distressing one; people making anxious inquiries thronged the thoroughfares leading to the 'hospitals, and the medical staff afforded all faclitie.s for identification. Twenty people who were admitted there injured, have since died, including a soldier. and several persons who were supposed to have been in the gallery and second circle. To gain anything like a fair conception of the d.read- fel struggle foe life which took place, one has to picture up a panic-stricken throng of men, women, and 'children pushing or forcibly impelled towards a single doorway, the only exit the gallery seems to have afforded, and followed by tongues of dame momentarily increasing until at last the outer fringe of the erna.ss was overtaken by it. This contact of the names with the people, it must be borne in mind, happened only a very few minutes after the discovery of the outbreak, and within but little more time than it takes to write the fact, the majority of the people whose corpses have been recovered had breathed their last. In fact, the suddenness of the affair is at the same time its saddest and most satisfac- tory feature. It is sad to think that so many people were launched into eternity so suddenly, but it is consoling to remember that their "death agonies, though acute, were brief. As for those who escaped this furnace, they did so either over the bodies of their more unfortunate companions or through the windows. When the latter alternative was adopted the jumpers often flew from ono death to find another almost equally horrible, whilst others sustained fractures to their limbs. The great_ mass of the men, women, and children in the galleve were, however, wedged into an almost immovable masS, and the advancing flames roasted them to death.,

NEW 'YORE.lomnar.—The larger portion of the 'working men of this city abstained, frotti-workto.day in accordance with the Act passed last winter by-the State Legislature, -making the first. Monday in September a legal holiday, to he called "Labour day." The various other labour organisations united in a parade, which was reviewed by Henry George and other labour leaders. It waspromised that there would be 60,000inen irt line, but there were really less than 20,000. Thomost•noticeable feature of therroarch past the reviewing stand ,was the ref mod of a large portion of the working men to salute Henry George. L-Some refused to•cheer him, and others displayed positive rudeness, the .bands,ceasing-to play, and the banners being furled. This conduct is due to Henry George's,ceurse in excluding-the Socialists from his labour party in the present campaign. He did it in the hope of thus attracting the farmers' vote in the country divisien, but the general opinion is that he will not snowed bees:use the farmers dislike his land theories. The most encouraging thing about to-day's parade is the indications that Aare given that the working men..are beginning to tire Of Henry George and his teachings, and to split into warring factions.

The first seven persons brought out were pronounced to be dead by Mr. Kempe, a surgeon, who stood at, the front of the fire escape, in ordertio examine each body. The laboursof the rescuers were incessant—they found people of both sexes and of all ages huddled together in the utmost confusion, and though every now and then a grim kind of cheer greeted the‘Mtimation that in wome body there was a sign of life, yet in the gnat traejority of instances there was un- happily no room for hope. 'The yard of the 'New London Hotel close by noon be- Tame a veritable chuniel house. There lay row after row of corpses nearly a hundred in number. The faces df some of these were blmkened almost beyond recogni- tion, and others again were stained with blood that had lowed from thermouth and nostrils irithe death struggle The clothes of .most of the victims were scorched or -tattered, and in 'some instances they had been torn oft bodily, whilst some of the unfortunate people seemed as though they were but asleep. The comitenances of others bore deep traces of the agony they had endured. One young girl who was taken into the yard betrayed slight signs sfillfe, and the surgeons aid ill they could to recall consciousness, but inc few moments they were obliged to confess that the last lingering ray of life had departed. There was a band eif willing workers aiding the medical•gentlemen as Pad, case was 'taken into the yard, but unhappily in most of them human aid was of no avail. The yara was kept :as free from crowding as possible, 'but some anxious friends .of victims who pleaded for admission wore allowed to enter, and now and 'then a wail of lamentation ,announced the discovery of a dead relative. Ac rrriage shed in which bodies were placed soon 'became too 'limited, and the stables had to be utilised. A muriber of Town Councillors who were present ordered Shell coffins to be made at once, and as these werq completed the bodies were one by one removed to the public rooms, there to await re- cognition in cases where They had not been already recognised. The strong men -who were so willingly assisting in removing bodies, Siokened over their dread- ful taSk, and everyone was horror-stricken, being hardly able to realise the awful .extent of the calamity. THE AWFUL GALTJERY STRUGGLE.

The accounts first published as to the disaster rather understated than overestimated the loss of life Little doubt now exists that 250 persons have perished in the flames. The cause of the fire still remains unascertained ; but universal testimony is korne by those who were in the theatre at the time to the lightning-like rapidity with which the flames spread. It is difficult to conceive, and yet the fact is verified on all band, that within ten minutes of the first alarm, the interior of the theatre was one mass of fire, which licked alike pit, dress circle, upper circle, and gallery. In nearly all cases death arose from suffocation, and not from burning. 'Quite 'five.sixths of the victims perisbed in the staircase leading from the gallery to the street. This staircase—the only means of exit from the gallery—was of stone, with stone walls, and having an iron railing running along on one side. It had distinct turns, and was in fact a spiral -staircase. The result was that as the people madly rushed down they got hopelessly jammed and crushed at eacheturn. In the frantic attempts to free themeelves the limbe of some appear to have been torn off, and of others fractured. At each turn in the staircase was found a sickening pile of charred human remains. A high post about halfway down the winding staircase was another fatal obstruction to the free passage of the panic-stricken crowd. But for two windows in the stair- case very few indeedivould•have escaped. One ef thrse windows opened on to tbe leader; the other overlooked the , street. Several climbed out Of there and jumped to the ground, a depth of fourteen feet, or were rescued by fire. escapes. Out of the 'l9O persons, known to have been in the gallery, very (few got out by the door. Surprise and even indignation is expressed that in a modern theatre there should have been but one exit from the gallery, and that of such an unsatisfactory character. The scene Is described by those who witnessed the fire as heartrending. The shrieks of the unhappy victims rose in their shrill agony above the crackling and hissing of the devouring flames, and the dull thud of falling masonry and timber, and it is stated that the thrilling notes of human despair were dis- tinctly beard a mile away from the scene of the disaster. Many of the bodies brought out are mutilated and burned to such a frightful degree that recognition was impossible. In some cases, only beeps of charred remains have been found, and now and then the searchers have brought out a stray arm or leg, with the flesh burnt off to the bone. The bodies and remains of those recovered are lying in rows in the shed and stable of the London Hotel ; and the sight is one horrible in the extreme. The faces of some of the vic- tims are frightfully contorted ; others, whetter pallid faces and thickened foam issuing from the mouth indicate death from suffocation, present a more composed appearance ; but in very many cases the bodies are charred beyond all hope of earthly recognition. Throughout fuesday the stable yard of the hotel has been the scene of sorrow and lamentation, which words can at best ill-describe. MESSAGE 'FROM THE QUEEN. On Tuesday evening, the following message was received from the Home Secretary on behalf of the Queen :—" By command of her 'Majesty,! ask von to express her Majesty's deep symeeethy with the injured in last night's accident, and with the families of those who have been killed.--intenr MATTHEWS, Home Secretary." RELIEF FUND OPENED. _ . _ _ _

At a meeting of held on Tuesday even- ing. a vote of condolence with the relations of the victims of the fire was passed, and a relief fund opened. £4OO or £5OO was subscribed, including £lOO lions the Hon. H. S. Northcote Various calculations have been made as to the amount of funds that will be necessary to render anything like ade- quate assistance, but it may be taken, speaking generally, that from £lO,OOO to £20,000 will he required. A fund has been opened at the Mansion House, London. and up to six o'clock ors Thursday evening upwards of £2,000 bad been subscribed. THE IN QUESC. At the inquest, on Tuesday, the jury having viewed the bodies, which presented a most sickening eight, the Coroner intimated that on sanitary grounds heshould issue a general order for the interment of all who had been identified, and ales for the burial of the remains which were beyond the possibility of recognition. Evidence was taken to the eaect that the number of bodies now in the hotel yard was, as nearly as could be judged, 1t0; six others had died in the hospital. Witnesses were then called who identified the dead. The scene in the room was a most painful one, the spacious chamber being crowded with weeping relatives. It would be difficult to bestow doo much praise on the mem- bers of the medical profession ss Exeter. Punctually at eleven o'clock the city coroner (Mr. H. W. 'Hooper) re-opened the court of inquiry at the New London Hotel, and further evidence was taken as to the identity of the dead. After this the jury walked to the theatre close at hand, and inspected the gallery staircase. Dr. E. C. Bell, consulting surgeon at the Devon and Exeter Hospital, ac- companied the jurymen and pointed out to them the spots where it was obvious from the number of bodies found that blocks had taken place. He likewise showed the positions in which the dead were discovered. The brickwork of the theatre remains almost intact, though Its internal fittings are reduced to ashes. Very little iron seems to have been used in the structure. In fact, with the exception of some four or five iron supports that are still standing in grim loneliness, there was none. The jury concluded their in- rpm ion of the building and then proceeded to the Exeter and Devon Hospital to see the eight bodies there await- ing an inquest. In addition to these there are 4e3 trunks of bodies so dreadfully charred, burnt up, and dismembered as to render recognition impossible. Altogether, 114 bodies or portions of bodies were laid out in the New London Hotel yard, and adding the eight victims who died at the hospital we have a I total of 122, as representing the loss of life so far as can at present be definitely ascertained. There is little doubt that many bodies still lie buried in the debris which strews the basement of the building. This is the opinion everywhere entertained, and looking to the fact that many people are, ,till missing it is safe to predict that the loss of life fhvolved in this catastrophe amounts to at least 150. The most important witness examined during the progress of the inquest on Wedneeday morning was Dr. Bell, who I gave detailed evidence as to the number of bodies that had I been recovered from the theatre. Especially in- teresting was the information which Dr. Bell gave as to the cause of death. It is consoling to know that in the vast majority of cases death arose from suffocation, and that the awful injuries and discolouratien of which the bodies afford such evidence were in all probability caused after death. In a few cases death was the result of pres- sure in the terrible struggle th.at took place on the staircase in the rush for the door. One singular feature in the doctor's evidence was his assertion that the larger proportion of bodies bore traces of ecalds, and not burns. These he attributed to the action of the water that the firemen poured upon the building, heated, as it had become after contact with the dames. The in- quest was adjourned shortly after two o'clock. The future sittings' it was stated, will be held at the Guildhall. Be- fore the jurors separated they were informed by the Coroner that their attention would next be directed to by far the most important part of the inquiry—viz., a!" to when, how, and by what means the sari affair took place." The jury are to meet again on Friday. It was hinted by the Coroner that it was by no means improbable that aGovern- ment officer would be sent down to investigate the matter, and strict instructions were given that the steps leading to the gallery should not be touched. SERIOUS ANTI-SOCIALIST DISTURBANCE AT RUT I E R DAM.

ROTTERDAM, THURSDAT.—A somewhat serious anti. Socialist disturbance occurred in this city last night. M. Domela Nienwenhats, the 6ccialist leader who was recently released from prison, arrived here last night, accompanied by several of his followers, in order to attend a reception which had h een organised ia his hangar by the Rotterdam Socialists at the People's Cuf.e. house. A large crowd assembled in front of the establishment, and prevented M. Nienwenhuis from alighting from his carriage, so that the police were cons.. pelted to form a cordon round the vehicle in order to enable the b'eciatiet leader and his friends to ente- the coffee•house. The crowd then commenced throwing stones at the win- dows, and tore down the red dag displayed over the door, afterwards burning it in the square before the police station. The mob thee Attempted to force an entrance into the coffee house, and the ,police had to charge the crowd to prevent a serious riot. Order was not restored until nearly mid. i,eight.

'Board of Guardians, had directed that the ceremony should take placeat four o'clock, and long before that hour hun- dreds of people, a large proportion of whom were dressed In black, were to be seen weeding their way along the high- road to the scene of interment. A large crowd assembled in front of the mortuary chapel, were for the time being had been laid the bodies of the unidentified victims. At the grave there could not have been less than 2,008 persons assembled. The ceremony was a long one, inas- much as the bodies had to be interred In four batches. and this necessitated the burial service being read four different times. It was not till aim o'clock that the sad rites over the unidentified dead bad been concluded. Only the uniden- tified were buried on Wednesday. . .

Early on Thursday it was known at the Higher Ceme- tery that some 19 or 20 interments would take place in the afternoon. The Cathedral bells' mournful tolling seemed like the echo of the city's beartful sorrow, loading the very air with melancholy. Nearly every house in the city ex- hibited some token of mourning, those persons who happily had no reason to lament the loss of personal friends show- ing the sympathy for others in the terrible calamity which has desolated so many homes. On most of the flag-staffs in the city colours were flown half-mast, window blinds, especially those of houses along the principal approaches to the cemetery, were drawn, and there was hardly a trades- man's establishment that did not by means of shutters con- vey an intimation of the solemn proceedings ef the after- noon to passere.by. Thousands lined the thoroughfares leading to the cemetery. Within the graveyard, a yet deeper melancholy prevailed. A large number of graves had been prepared, over thirty men having been at work all day excavating them, and even while the first bodies were being interred lahourers were busy with pick and' shovel making ready more narrow beds. The scenes at the grave sides were deqly affecting, and but few present sought to hide their grief. As the body of Joseph Dart was lowered into its last resting place a woman standing by exclaimed " Poor Joe, his wife has not been found yet." "And his children," said another weeping weman, "three of them, and one a cripple; God help them." Scenes like this were common enough all over the ceme- tery. Bombardier Scattergood, of the Royal Artillery, was buried with military honours, over 150 cff the deceased's comrades being present, with detachments of the Devon- shire Regiment and militia. During the day the work of examining the debris has been actively progressing in the theatre. On Wednesday 'night the charred remains of an infant were recovered, they I having fallen through into the Ufa. During the morning further human bones were discovered, and this afternoon in a small room off the passage leading from the refreshment room to the foyer, which room was at the time of the tire used for storage purposes, were found the remains of a man and woman. AN IMPORTANT LEri:ER.

In a letter addressed to the City Coroner, on Wednesday night, Colonel Sir F. C. Firth, chief officer of the Fire Bri- gades Aeaociation, says: "I have completed my inspection of the theatre, and lam at once communicating with the Rome Secretary to the following effect, namely, that had the Exeter theatre possessed what is known as a mechanical brigade,,alias a pateut automatic sprinkler over the various ceilings or simply over the stage part, the disaster would have been prevented, because it would have stopped the fire with its shower baths whilst it was yet possible tor the skill of man to do so. I hope the Fire Brigades Association will succeed, with the support sof public opinion, in inducing Parliament before being prorogued to pass a temporary bill insisting on all theatres within three moaths adopting a mechanical fire brigade. Some theatres have already done so. I know a cotton factory company who have adopted the protection and no longer insure, thereby saving between £l,OOO and £2,000 per year in premiums." In conversation to-night I asked Sir Charles Firth's opinion of the construction af the gallery staircase, and he replied: —"I cannot approve of it, of course. lam certain that in a new theatre like that it would have been a great improve- ment to have done away with all landings. Instead of hav- ing a lew steps and then a landing, it would be much better for the steps to be continuous. In the crash and confusion the people, when they get on these landings, do not know where to had the next step, and consequently they stumble and fall. I would do away with steps altogether as they have done in the leadidg railway stations, aud go in for inclines."

div.head: IRELAND.
div.p: IRELAND.

A publican Of Waterford, named Britton, was drowned whilst bathing in Tramore Bay, on Sunday. Information has been received at Lismore of an attack by moonlighters on the residence of Major Chearnley, J.P.,Balter=bridge, county Waterford. Mrs. Chearnley frightened them away by firing a revolver. The eviction of a man named Frost, with his wife and 10 children, was carried out on Monday at Rossmaher, county Clare, by the sub-sheriff and a detachment of armed policemen. Attempts had previously been made to carry out the eviction, but without effect. Opposi- tion was now offered, the sub-sheriff being attacked by Frost's son, and struck on the hand with a pitchfork. A quantity of dirty water was also thrown over the party. Frost and two of his sons were arrested and conveyed to gaol. Lord Portarlington writes in the Freeman's Journal., ap- proving Archbishop Walsla's proposal with regard to the land question. Be adds: "Landlords and tenants are partners in the same firm, and should itbe best for the in- terests of the nation at large that such partnership should be dissolved, then it should be for both parties to consider together how such termination of their partner- ship can be best carried out, to their mutual advantage." He thinks, however, that the conference should be de- ferred till after the publication of a Government land purchase scheme.
THE CORK POISONING CASE.--A SECOND EXHUMATION.

Dr. Cross was again brought up on Monday at Cork, charged with the murder of his wife by poisoning her at Shandy Hall. Additional interest was taken in the pro- ceedings owing to the circumstance that the body of Mrs. Cross had, since the last adjournment, been taken for the second time out of the grave, and portions of the remains taken away by the doctors for analysis. There had been some rumours afloat as to the prisoner being in 9 prostrate condition, but he appeared as formerly, look- ing very well, and taking a keen interest in the pro- ceedings. Miss Cross, his sister, again sat by his side. The court and precincts were crowded. The deposi- tions of Miss Jefferson, a Protestant Sister of Mercy, were first'resd over. This lady was on a visit to the deceased lady at Shandy Hall up,to the day of her death. She now added to her evidence that she saw the body laid out. It was merely laid straight, hut witness did , not express surprise, thinking it might be the local cus- tom not to do any more than this.—Dr. Pearson was then further examined. He deposed that he had made further examinations of the organs of the body of deceased since his former evidence. He had found a minute quantity of strychnine, but not in a poisonous quantity. On the 23rd of last month he again examined the cofAn, which he opened at the grave. From the result of the examination , which followed this second exhumation he still adhered to ; his evidence that Mrs. Cross waS poisoned by arsenic, and that she did not die from a natural cause. He identified eel, tain packages of strychnine and arsenic found in Shandy Hall, which were handed to him for analysis.—Mr. Pool, manager of the North-Western Hotel, North Wall, Dub- lin, was examined, and deposed that Dr. Cross and the lady in tAe photograph produced (Mrs. Cross, then Miss Skinner) came to the hotel at the end of March last. They came again on three subsequent occasions, includ- ing the 21st of April. Mary Smith, chambermaid at the North-Western Hotel, deposed to seeing Dr. Cross and the lady shown in the photograph come to the hotel in March. They slept in room No. 3, which was a single-bedded room. They also came on the 21st April, and on the 21st and 24th June. On each occasion they passed as man and wife.—A labourer in the employ of Dr. Cross and the postmaster at Coachford were examined to prove that letters had been sent by Dr. Cross to Miss Skinner after she left Shandy Hall. The postmaster stated that setters came directed "to be left Lill called for," with initials which he could not make out on the corners of them. Dr. Cross came flr them and got them.—This concluded the evidence. The depositions were then read over to the accused, and on being ellarged and -•nutioned by the magistrate, he said': "I am jest as innocent of that murder or of that accusa- tion as you are, or any man in this room." A formal application to admit the prisoner to baikwas refused.. THE NATIONALIST DEMONSTRATION.

There was a great preparation in Ennis ou Saturday, both by the authorities and the people, for the meeting an- nounced to be held on Ballycoree Hill on Sunday afternoon and subsequently proclaimed by the Government. Crowds of people from all parts of county Clare gathered in the town, and there :also arrived a troop of hussars, the Lein- stet Regiment of infantry, some members of the Army Medical Staff with their appliances, and 500 armed police. In the evening Messrs. T. D. Sullivan, William ()Brien, Dillon, Cox, and Sheehy, members of the Irish Parlia- mentary party, accompanied by the Hon. P. Stanhope, M.P. for Wednesbury, reached Ennis from Dublin. A•meeting was held in the street, undisturbed by the police. Mr. Stan- hope said he brought a mersage of peace and goodwill from the democracy of Great Britain, who cordially endorsed the Idemands of the Irish people. In the opinion of every right- ' thinking man accross the Channel, the meeting which bid been proclaimed was one which they were legally entitled to bold. He hoped that by their firm and constitutional at- titude on the morrow the men of Clare would maintain for themselves and their sympithisers the right of freedom of speech. Mr. Dillon also urged the people, by an orderly and peaceful bearing, to deprive the Government of every shadow of excuse for the outrage on popular liberty which they were contemplating. The Government were trying to suppress the meeting because otherwise they could not carry on their policy of eviction and rack-rent, and also because they were alarmed at the sight of English members carrying Personally to Ireland the assurance of the sympathy and sapport of the people of England. On Sunday the Whorl- ties carried oat their promise of prever,ting a meeting on Ballycoree Hill, but, nevertheless, a meeting was held, just outside Ennis. A great procession was formed in the town and halted on the highroad. Addresses were delivered, from a vehicle by Mr. Sullivan, Mr. Stantiop, and Mr. O'Brien. When the speaking was nearly over, a body of hussars ap- proached, and Colonel Turner ordered the crowd to dis- perse. Mr. Stanhope protested that what they were doing was legal and Constitutional, but he and his fellow M P.'s advised the people to depart quietly. This counsel was ac- cepted, and the people returned to Ennis apparently well satisfied with the [incest% of their demonstration.

EIGHT MEN KILLED. On Tuesday afternoon, while a gun jacket, weighing about 30 tons, was being amt at the works of hiessrs. Vickers, Sons, and Co., Sheffield, the mould, containing 26 tons of ni:Aten steel, suddenly exploded, scattering the liquid metal in all directions, wrecking the building, and hurling several of the workmen long distances. Four men were got out of the dêbrss dead, and a fifth was found to be in such a position that several hours elapsed before he could be extricated, while six other men, badly muti- lated and with broken limbs, were conveyed to the Sheffield Infirmary. Three of these have since died, and a fourth is not expected to recover. The killed are Job Holland, the foreman, who was almost decapitated ; Willi4tti Glavis, shockingly mutilate 4 ; Henry Walker, Henry Woodhall, Frederick Colson, John Murray, Samuel Edge, antlJames Ellis; the last three dying at the infirmary. Woodhall was em- ployed in another department, but had gone to the fore- man with a message, and the foreman himself had only returned from a holiday on Saturday. The Cause of the accident is unknown, knit, it is supposed that the metal came in contact with inoistrrre. .

Another account says that an immense steel nPot, weighing 50 tons, intended for a gun jacket, exploded. with a report heard for miles. Between 20 and 30 workmen were employed in the melting-house, and of these eight were killed and 12 others injured, some, tt is feared, fatally. The dead include the manager of the department and three assistant. ,
THE LIBERAL LEAGUE.-MR. MAUDE'S
SECESSION.

A fate and demonstration, under the auspices of the Liberal League, took place on Monday at Alexandra Palace. The weather militated against the attendance, and a comparatively small number were present. & conference was held to consider the political situation. and the duty of the Liberal League and kindred as.socia. tons. Mr. T. Eccleston Gibb occupied the chair at the com- mencement. Several letters were read by Mr. J. D. Digby from Mr. Gladstone, Sir Geo. Trevelyan, the Mar- cans of Ripon, Sir W. Plowden, and several M.P.s, ex- pressing regret at their inability to attend. A resolution was carried in favour of establishing Leagues in Ireland wherever National League lodges were prohibited or suppressed.—Mr. Maude, Mr. Howell, M.P., and others, supported the resolution. Sneaking of the Liberal Unionists,. Mr. Howell threw on them the blame of defeating Mr. Gladstone's Govern- ment, and advised the constitutionalists to remember that at the next general election. At the luncheon, Mr. Shirley, M.P., presided; and Mr. MAUDE, in proposing the toast of "Our Liberal Legis- lators," stated his reasons for seceding from the Liberal and Radical Unionists, for whom he fermerly acted as secretary. Those reasons were, he mid firstly, that the policy of combination that called itself the Unionist party seemed to him dangerously retro- grade in its nature, and inconsistent with the pledges given at the General Election; secondly,. that the concessions made by Mr. Gladstone to the- Radical Unionist objections to his policy last year, bad removed all excuse for opposing the programme of the Liberal party; and, thirdly, that the change wrought in the attitude of the Irish Nationalists towards this country by Mr. Gladstone's proposals was such as to en- courage the Liberal Party to entrust them with the re- sponsibility of the administration of Irish affairs through a more constitutional machinery than the branches of the National League. They had to choose between the policy of hope and the policy of des`pair. The time had now come for plain speaking. For his own part, he should not be there if he did not believe that the leaders of the National League were prepared to accept as a final settlement the generous measure of Home Rule the Liberals were willing to help to attain. (Hear, hear.) Under these circumstances, why should they not join with the Liberal party in the farmulation of a Home Rule scheme? (Bear, hear.) Nothing would do more to clear the issue to be fought out next session, and to rally to their standard every citizen with a spark of democratic feel- ing than the conviction that the Irish policy they were fighting for would never be repudiated as the work of Saxon statesmen, and was as freely accepted as a final settlement by the representatives of the Irish party as by the Liberal party. Let the next Home Rule scheme be presented as an ultimatum to Parliament and the country on the joint responsibility of Mr. Gladstone and Mr. ParnelL The sense of fighting in the dark for a. measure of doubtful finality would then be removed, and lie believed such reunion of the Liberal party would en- able them to sweep the Government from Downing- street and the Tory majority from Parliament (Loud cheers.)

div.head: TERRIBLE SHIPWRECKS.-LOSS OF 32. LIVES.
div.p: TERRIBLE SHIPWRECKS.-LOSS OF 32. LIVES.

The smack Cygnet, of Yarmouth, William Skoyles, master, landed at Yarmouth port. on Saturday night five of the crew of the iron fourenasted ship, Falls of Bruer, of Glasgow, Captain Edwards. master, the other mem- bers of the crew, 24 in number, having been lost with the vessel on:Friday, 25 miles nff Yarmouth. It appears that the ship, which was 1,742 tons register, was laden with salt from H.,mburg for Calcutta, and that she encountered the heavy gale of Friday. During one of the squalls some of her sails wore -blown away, her cargo shifted, and she was thrown on her beam ends ,and sank. The crew had only time to cut away two of the boats, ono of which instantly smashed, and the other drifted away bottom upwards. Three of the crew, named John Herech Moller, Hans Haildoeser (Germans), and William Hoghtlnd (a Russian Finn), swam, to the upturned boat and got on her keel, and subsequently, as she righted, got into her, and baled out the water as well as they could. Two others, named Johannes Kama and Lars Peter Jonssen, both Swedes.. floated on pieces of the wreckage for six or seven hours. They continued in this perilous position from nine in the morning until four in the afternoon, when they were seen by the smack Cygnet, which bore down and rescued them cc ith great difficulty. The men by that time were in an extremely exhausted condition. On being landed on Saturday night at Yarmouth they were taken to and cared for at the sailors' home. There, is no doubt that the rest of the crew, with a pilot who was on board,, were drowned, as no other vessel was seen by the crew of the Cygnet near the scene of the wreck, and no ems else was picked up, although the smack remainedlcruie- ing around the spot for several hours. • One of the crew of the Belfast barque Star of Scotia has arrived at Liverpool, and lies given some very thrill- ing details of the wreck of that vessel on the Falkland Islands and the loss of eight lives. Of the unfortunate men drowned one was the mate of the vessel, and of the others-the bodies of two were found on the beach with nearly all the flesh eaten off by. the wild and voracious birds that frequent the place. According to the amount of the seaman who arrived at, Liverpool, and whose name is Martin Olsen, it appears that the Star of Scotia was bound from San Fransisco to Queenstown for orders and had on board a cargo of wheat. She was manned by a crew of 22 hands all told, and got ashore on the rocks at Bull Point, about 100 miles from Port Stanley, Falkland Islands. It was about half-past 11 at night when the vessel struck,, and the crow remained on board until daylight. The captain with the majority of the crew got away in one boat, and the second boat was in charge of Mr. Frazer, the mate. The captain's boat was the first to reach the shore, but the mate's boat was cast on the beach by the heavy surf. and in it were the semi-conscious forms of two of the crew—viz.' an Englishman and a Scotchman natarsi Davis and Drummond. The mate was also in the boat, but the poor fellow had just breathed his last. It seems that while making for the shore the boat was cap- sized no less than seven times, until there were only three at the occupants left—viz., the mate, Drummond, and Devitt. When the shipwrecked men landed the island was covered with entice, Ma the place altogether was bitterly cold. They, however, found shelter in the hut of some herdsmen, and were as kindly treated as possiblq. The herdsmen also rode 100 miles to inform the authori- ties of the disaster. The men lost their clothes, and had to remain on the island for a month before they were taken 4, wav by a German mail steamer and subsequently transferred to an English steamer.

THE EXPLOSION AT A GUNPOWDER WORKS.—Tke fleC)ad man who was injured by an explosion at the Lowwood Gun- powder Works in Furness died on Thursday morning. The two mem who were killed were working on the crown wheel. e !An one of them struck fire with the implement with which he was working, and it is tupposed th it this ignited the powder lodges in the crevices, thus cau sing a esrfoas explosion. PRIZE FIGHT IN WALES.—Another prize fight Was CIL Thursday reported from Penycoed, where the combatints were two miners, hailing from Forth and Pontypridd. The conflict took place in a secluded spot, and was witnessed by a large number of spectators. Twenty-three rounds were fougtt, and the struggle, which was a fierce one, lasted 40 minutes, beth men being eeverely bruised. The police ace in pursuit of the pugilists.

ATAL FINE IN CO N . —Early on Thursday morning a tire occurred in a house at Hampstead-road, London, let cut as a shop and tcnemente. At the tints of the outbreak about twenty persons were sleeping in the vatioua rooms upstairs, and 'tuna,: very exciting scenes were witnessed as these wore rescued. Two cr three were injured in escaping from the burning building, and the son of a lodger, named Williams. who lived on the second floor, was subsequently found to have been burnt to death. Tan Bomar STinau.—The President of the Board of Trade has written to Canon Atkinson. vicar of Bolton and rural dean, who bis interested himself to brine about a settlement of the dispute, upon the question whether Mr. Burnett, of the Labour Serum would be allowed to act as arbitrator for the men. The communication expresses re- gret that the Board of Trade are unable to allow Mr. Bur- nett to act for the men, it being considered inadvisable thst a Government official should so act. ALLEGED MCILDEE OF A CIIILD.-A blacksmito named William Hunter we a•inlitted to the Carlisle Infirmary t Thursday evening suffering from severe wounds, self-in- flicted, in the throat. Hunter had been tramping from Wigton with a woman minted Steele and her daughter, a child four years old. On the road Hunter, angered at the child's conduct, kicked it with such violence that it died soon afterwards. The man then cut his throat with a inoket-knite, and is not expected to recover.

The sum and ‘tQ atce of the Vice Chairman's reply is that, °Ming to his judgment, the Library Corn-

IT is due to the present Parliament to say that it has done its duty in one direction, and that is in amending the law so as to make certain fraudulent practices in trade punish- able by fine and imprisonment. By greatly reducing, if not entirely suppressing, the I more unscrupulous tricks of trade, the new Merchandise Marks Law Consolidation and Amendment Act, as it is called, will be the means of giving the honest dealer a better ; chance in the market than he has hitherto had. Take the watch trade for example; English 1 watches have a high reputation for excellent workmanship, and it is a matter of course to say that, other things being equal, our own neo-1 pie at any rate would prefer an English watch to any other. Buyers, to be sure, I want to get a good thing cheap, and to meet this desire certain dealers have for a long ; time been in the habit of putting inferior foreign movements in English hall-marked cases, and palming them off as English ! watches. It was a fraud on the face of it to do such a thing; for in ninety-nine instances out I of a hundred the buyers who troubled them- selves to see that cases were stamped with ; the Eneliqh hall-mark, would have refused to take the watch purchased had they known that, whilst the case was English, the works I were foreign. It is in this way that the I home watch trade has greatly suf- fered, and that the workmen of Pres- I cot and the neighbourhood have for some time been on the borders of starva- tion. They have suffered in pocket and in I reputation, for it has unfortunately happened that the defects of inferior foreign-made movements have been set down to bad work- manship on the part of our countrymen. The worst of it was that as the law stood there was nothing for it but to "grin and 'bide;" but under the new Act a dealer who plays tricks of this kind will be liable to imprison- ment or a heavy fine. For instance, if a tradesman sold a watch as one of English make which proved to be English only as to case, he would incur on conviction the risk of being sent to prison for two years. Then in the matter of Cases sent to be assayed, a declaration has now to be made as to the country or place in which they have been made, and int proves that they have been manufactured out of the United Kingdom they are to be marked so as to indicate that they are not of English make. The law, too, gives ample protection for what are known as Sheffield goods. It has been the cirstom with a considerable number of firms in Sheffield and Birmingham to receive hard- ware manufactured on the Continent, but stamped, on arriving in England, with the trade mark of the English firm and sold as articles of English make. It is hardly neces- sary to say that these g•oods are not equal to those of genuine English make; they are for the most part " cheap and nasty ;" and, not only so they are the means of keeping Euglish workmen idle and at the same time of bringing English workmanship into bad repute. It is the watch dodge over again in a thousand ways. But the law sfeps in, and there will for the future be less of these vicious practices ; for the use of a trade mark which is misleading becomes a " false trade description" under the Act, and is pun- ishable by fine and imprisonment. The law, it should be added', applies to merchandise of all classes, so that if there is a false desbrip- tion as to "the number, quantity, measure, guage, or weight of any goods," the offender becomes subject to its lash. It is impossible, of course, to make people moral by Act of Parliament; but it is possible to restrict the operations of the flagrantly immoral, and
