"TOUCH AND GO"
In London, the other day, a Chinaman who was a witness took the oath by breaking a saucer. English witnesses—many of them at any rate—have another method; they kiss a book and then break—their word.

The Indian Budget is usually 'eft to the rush of business at the end of the session. But what matters, seeing that it affects the welfare of some 250 millions of people only? If they show themselves discontented, we can treat them as we do the Irish—ran thetn down with a Coercion Act.

There are some signs that the Tories, find- ing that the cry "Union in danger" edeites no interest, are disposed to go in for Protec- tion. The difficulty is that if they move at all they must do something for the farmers; hut subsidising the farmer means an increase in the price of the loaf of bread. This ugly fact stands in the way at present, and it wii)l continue to stand in the way, if we are not much mistaken.

Another and another Hood are required to sing "The Song of the Shirt." On Wednes- day an inquest was held in Holloway, Lon- don, resoecting the death of Mary Carr, a tailoress, aged 44. The evidence showed Ithat the deceased had died of starvation. Sue earned about half-a-crown a week, and her daughter earned between 6s. and 83 a week as a tie-maker. "Oh God! that bread should be so dear and fresh and blood so cheap."

The Warrington Town Council some time ago resolved that prices of contracts with the Corporation should be published; but from a question put at the meeting on Tuesday last, it would appear that the Gas Committee are violating this resolution. The committee say that it is not in the public inte(est to publish the prices; but that is a moot point, and the resolution stands in their way. The de- cision of the whole Council ought to be of greater weight than that of a committee, that is a section of the Council. But the com- mittee seem to be a law into themselves, and do as thtey like.

Nobody would subscribe to bring the wall down in front ot the Warrington Town Hall by way of celebrating the Queen's Jubilee, and it seems the majority in the Council will have none of it. Four hundred pounds is certainly totimuch to pay for the whistle. Happy thought ! How would it be if Sir Gilbert Greenall. instead of provid- ing a white elephant in the shape of a foun- tain, were to change his mind, and pay for the wall being knocked down. It migt:t be a good investment, seeing that one reason for taking the wall down is to improve the out- look of the Conservative Club. The ball given by the Mayor and Mayoress of Warrington, on Thursday night, was a big success. Old and young, following the ex- ample of host and hostess, appeared to lay themselves out for pleasing and being pleased. The parquette flooring was a novelty; it looked well and was found to be as good as it looked. In brief, everything was first class and seemed to say :
On with the dance, let joy be unconfined; No sleep till morn, when youth and pleapre meet To chase the glowing hours with flying feet.

There is one good story anent the ball which has the merit of being true. A cer- tain young tradesman of exalted ideas was early on in the week lamenting to a pro- fessional friend the fact that the assembly was (thanks to its being representative) likely to be of a mixed character. He almost regretted having accepted the invitation. " Are you going ? " asked his friend "Well, yes; he had accepted." "Really." was the cutting reply, "I wouldn't have ac- cepted had I known a lot of shopkeepers were going." [Exit "shopkeeper" meditating, with a crushed air, on the lesson he had re- ceived.]

A Correspondent, who signs himself" W," and whose communication reaches us too late to be included in our " Letters " column, writes as follows : "Our Mayor and Mayoress. Ought not their townspeople and friends to give them some special recogni- tion, the Mayor for his long services, and both for their splendid entertainment in this and former years? I suggest a public din- ner (ladies and gentlemen), followed by a conversazione and a portrait of the Mayoress to be placed in the Mayor's Parlour as a companion to his own."
The Liberals of Runcorn had a picnic to Winnington Hall on Saturday, and received a very hearty welcome from Mr. Brunt-I.r. The new member for the Northwich Divi-

sion mviie a thoroughly democratic speech. He believe,: in a Liberal Association being " a real live thing ;" and objects to members beinr appohmed at hole and corner meetings This is in ibe right vein, and it would be well if Liberal 3eaders in other constbuencies followed suit. They must 3klow themselves democratic, or they will lose touch with the people, and thus Ise electione.

IThe harrowing calastvophe at t- xeter points to the necessity of !stringent kgislatiln to ensure the safety of places of amosement. At present the Government have no a:lthority to interfere. It rests with local magi•Nrates in granting licenses to see that proper nrovi sion is made for the safety of the pubik; and it would seem that it does not do to utast to ' magisterial supervision. It is a difficult prob km to solve; but must be solved at what- ever cost. The Government, it wilt be obs,cA-ved, promise to aive their imme- diate attention to the subject.

Mr. Gladstone has been asked to be pre- sent at the Centennial of the Unites States, thus receiving the only invitation sent to any person not a citizen of that great country. Pressure of home affairs—that is to say the Home Rule question compels him to decline what he describes as the most flatter- ing proposal he has ever received. It' is generous of arc people of the United States to think of Mr. Gladstone in this connection, for they cannot have forgotten that he held aloof during the Civil War. But they rightly know and rightly revere the Grand Old Man.

LAUNCIEfiAT Rcrecoaw.—On Monday afternoon a coasting flit wan successfully leunched from the ship building yard of Messrs. Brundrit and Co., Runcorn. The vessel which has been built for the purpose of trading beetween Pen- maeninawr and Runcorn, was christened " Percy" by Master Percy Brundrit. It is 12 feet long, 19 feet 8 inches beam, and has a depth of hold of 8 feet 1 inch. The regia- tared tonnage of the tilt is 90 tons, hut the carrying capacity is estimated at about 160 tens. Built of English oak from the designs of Mr. John L. Davies, the craft is of the usual handsome and substantial character for which this firm is noted. and is an undoubted acquisition to Messrs. Brundrit's fleet. The rigging was fixed by Mr. Iblin Bates, tha sails were found by Mr. Samul Ravens- croft, and the painting was done by Mr. George Yarwood. of Church•etreet.

SCHOONER 617N1E AT BENCORN.—By the noon tide, on Saturday. the steam tug," Queen of the Alereey," belonging to the Manchester Ship Canal Company (Bridgewater Na- vigation Undertaking) was towing four vessels from Run- corn to Liverpool. Upon arriving opposite Ince the schooner Henry Holman grounded upon a sandbank at the edge of the deep channel, and had to be left there whilst the tug proceeded with the other vess4s. During the ebb-tide the schrioner remained in an upright position, but at midnight the flood tide caused the vessel to fall over on its aide, and the bilge was sm tat:led. Water rapidly poured through the breach thus made, but the crew, whp had been asleep, Suc- ceeded in getting into a small boat, and rowed to Runcorn. On Sunday the vessel was again boarded, and the ropes. anchor, rim. were brought away, as the venal appeared likely to become me complete wreck. The " Henry Holman" I belonged to Matthews, of Padetow, Cornwall. and wee laden with coal for Plymouth, Her registered tonnage was 154 tons.

NEW BLACK ASH FacKNACPI AT WIDNES.—The Widnes Alkali Company, Limit, htve now at work a monstre black ash furnace. The revolver of ordinary size measures at most 18,1 feet long, with a diameter of 12i feet. The I boiling-down pans connected with such a furnace measure 60 feet in length. Each charge contains four tons of salt cake, and some of these revolvers get though 18 tons of salt cake per day, and consume 13 cwt. of coal per ton of ' cake decomposed. The giant reyolyinz flu-once measures in length 30 feet, and has a diameter of 12 feet 6 inches. Inside length is 28. feet 6 inches, with a diameter of 11 feet 4 inches, It is lined witli 16000 fire-bricks and 120 fire- clay blocks or breakers weighing 1± cwt. The bricks weigh per 1,000 about four tons. The weight of salt cake per charge (i e., contained in each charge of salt c:ke, lime- stone, mud, and slack) is 8 tons 12 cwt. For 100 tons of salt cake charged, there are also charged about 110 tons of lime, mud, and limestone, and 55 tons of mixing slack. In a week of seven days about 48 charges are worked through, weighing of raw materials about 25 tons per charge. The amount of salt cake decomposed weekly is about 400 tons,and may be reckoned as yielding 240 tons of 60 per cent. caustic soda. Fuel may be put down as 200 tons per week,or about 10 cwt. per ton of salt cake decomposed. Also with regard to the concentration of licisor from 20 deg. Tw. to 50 deg. Tw. there is sufficient of such concentrated liquor evapora- ted down to keep three self-fired caustic pots working.which are boiled at a strength of 80 deg. Tw.—Oil and Colour Man's' Journal.

Tnorrisia Hatente tr AT WIRNES —A trotting handicap promoted by Mr. J. Barrow, of the Albert Hotel, Widnes, took place at Millaeld• Recreatios Grounds on Monday atm noon The event was confined to tradesmen and others residing within a radius of three miles of Widnes. and prizes of £5, £l, and 10s were offered for competition, There were seventeen entries, and the race was run in heats the distance being a mile and a quarter, or four times round the course. The handicappers were Mr. James Burrows and Mr. Bill, butchers, and Mr. Robert Herriman, of the Mersey Hotel. The jadges were Messrs. P. Smith (Run- corn), R. Herriman, and T. Edwardson, mineral water manufacturer. A rather unpleasant dispute arose eat of the first heat, the driver of Mr. James Smart's Silence (scratch) alleging that the course had only been traversed three times, and the fact that the distance was accomplished in three minutes one second supported his contention. The judges. howewr, decided that the proper distance had been covered. The heats resulted as follows:—Heat 1, Mr. A. Quinn's Brown, Mare, 14 hands, 300 yards start; heat 2, Mr. J Horabin's Ginger Beer, 14 hands, 250 yards start; beat 3, Mr .1 Twigg's Stoleaway, 14i hands, 100 yards start; heat 4, Mr. F. Simcock's Old Paddy, 14 hands, 150 yards start: heat 5, Mr. J. Smith's O'd Mare, 14 hands, scratch; heat 6, Mr. G. Davidson's Hector, 14 hands, 280 yards start. The trial heats resulted in Davidson's Hector, Quinn's Brcwn Mare, and Twigg's Stoleaway being left to compete in the final. Hector came in first, half a length in front of Quinn's Mare, Stoleaway close up being third. Time, 4 min. 19 sec. Galloping was very palpably indulged in, and an objection was raised by the rider of Stoleaway. We understand the final is to be run over again on Monday. WIDNES TEMPERANCE DEMONSTRATION.—It bad been intended to hold a demonstration of the united temperance bodies of Widnes on Saturday afternoon, but awing to the very unfavonrable weather the demonstration was not car- ried out. On Saturday morning the meteorological appear- ances were decidedly favourable, but mid-day had been barely reached when rain set in and heavy showers fell with very little intermission during the whole of the afternoon. The first item on the projected programme was a meeting of the various temperance branches on Mersey Promenade, and this part of the proceedings was carried out in spite of the rain. After sheltering some time in the Free Church Sunday School. the weather brightened up a little. and a Procession was formed in order to walk to Appleton House, the residence of Mrs. Deacon, where a field was to be the scene of the day's operations. The following I order was taken :—United Methodist Free Church Band of Hope, Farnworth Wesleyan Band of Hope, the Whines Sec- tion of the Lifeboat Crew Division of the Sons of Temper- ance. Hutchinson-street Primitive Methodist Band of Hope, the Farnworth Branch of the C.E.T.S., the "Hops of AD- piston Lodge, Lacey-street Weseiyan Band of Hope, the, Baptist Band of Hope. the Independent Order of Realm- bites, and the "Lily" and "Samaritan" Lodges. These I numbered, in the aggregate, about 800, the total number which had been expected being 1,200. Three societies, how- I ever, which had been expected, the Albert-road. Weelevan Band of Hope, the junior branch of the Independent Order of Rechabites, and the "Onward" Lodge, did not put in an appearance. The procession was beaded by the Wesleyan Brass Band, and the Widnes Jubilee Temperance Brass Hoed was also present. The procession, however, had not been I long in motion when the rain fell so heavily that various branches began to fell away from the procession and make their way as rapidly as possible to their respective schools or lodgeroome, and the gathering was in this way com- pletely broken up. Several cf the societies had tea served at their own headquarters, and we understand that an out- door meeting was afterwards held by the lodges who had tea in Mali's Tempnarce Hall. The united demonstra- tion was, however, abandoned.

Heald and Mr. John Brock, at Widnes Petty Sessions. on Thurs- day, Robert Herrimtn, landlord of the Mersey Hotel, was summoned by the Widnes Local Board for illegally wasting water.—The defendant pleaded guilty.—Mr. J. T. Allen, who prosecuted, said the defendant had a bowling green attached to his house, and some time ago he obtained per- mission fi om the Local Board to run water through a hose. pipe for the purpose of watering the green. Of coulee the defendant paid for the water, but their worships would readily understand that the water had to be used in a legitimate manner, and was not to be allowed to run all night Defendast committed an offence similar to the one with which he was now charged last year, and he was then told that on a repetition of the offence proceedings would be taken against him. On the night of the 29th June the Inertecter In the course of his duty found a considerable waste of water taking place in the West Bank district, and on examination he found a hose pipe lying on the defen- dant's green, and water was running through it full bore. At ten o'clock on the following night a similar state of affairs existed.—lnspector Barrow corroborated, and said the waste of water was 100 gallons per hour.—The defens dint said he paid for the water all the year round, but in winter be did not use it, while in dry weather he did need it. The hoeepipe was only half 'inch bore, and there could not consequently be an much weste.—Richard &nes, the barman, gave evidence that when water was rum on the green the hosepipe was in charge of either Mr. Berriman or himself. If the water had been wasted as stated; it had been turned on hy seine person who had no business to do so.— A fine of 203 and costs was imposed. PROPOSED CHANGER AT OREEPPAY ROAD BCHOOL.—DR., - NO3IIRATIONAL EDTVATR)N. 1 The Beard proceeded to consider how the vacancy at : Oreenway-road School; caused trya joud ) the ia filledresintiounpoLTMbiseg [Hutchinson, the head teacher, Chairman said it would ant be wiee to fill up the vacancy until the Board bed fleetly decided what the character Of the school was to be in the future. At present there was a preponderance of boys at that school, there being 170 boys and 49 girls in attendance, and a consideration of the goes. teen might result in the appointment of a master. As they • were aware the school had been hitherto worked as a stan- dart one echoel and it bad nat been a :mem,. The school had been epee for the space ef 18 months, and there was still annum of accommodation and that state of affairs was likely to continue so long as it remain, cl a standard one school. Under these circutnstances it would bee burden to the ratepayers. It was established as a standard one school at the suggestion of Her Meeesty'e Inspecthr, and he thought chat before the Board either decided to teach the higher standards, or convert it into a school for infants they had better hare an interview with that gentleman-. That course would also be more speedy- than to open a metres- pandence with the Education Department, and it was im- portant that the matter should be settled as early as poe- sible—Frither Fennelly asked would it not be- better t* decide neon a definite scheme and submit Ifee° the inspector. This would, he argued, save a great deal 'crams. Personally he was certain the Greenway-toad schcols would • not succeed until they were placed on the SAM footiovarthe denominational schools—until all the standards were- taught. At present the children whe had been examined' and passed in standard one had to-seek another school in which to finish their education. Let them be complete schools like other schools in town if they wanted them to suceeed.—Mr. Beckett said it was evident that neither of the two previous speakers laid gone intr . the mutter with regard to the cost of working schools; other- wise they would net have spoken in the way they lead. Their first thought should be what was the original inten- tion with which Greetwav-road schools were built. It ware a well-known fact that there was sofficient aecommodstion in the denominational echools for boys but not so for infants and girls, especially girls. The Education Department in- structed the Board to find accommodation, which they had done. There was no reason now to think there was not ac- commodation for boys in the denomiaational tschoole. They must not forget that hitherto the different denoneina- lions had provided tho education of the country free of cost to the ratepayers. and it was not right nor fair that for the sake of a hobby—it was perhaps nothing more at the present time—that the school bleeds should run con- trary to denominational teaching. If it could he plover!' that the teaching in the denominational schools was ineffi- cient lie wou'd quite agree with what had been said, but it could not be proved, because most of them knew that the grants this year had been very good all the way round. Ire eome schools they had earned the excellent grant, which spoke well for the education'of Runcorn.—Mr Beckett said he did not object to what had been done ; it had been no hindrance to denominational schools. Supposing the Beard adopted the method named by the chairman and vice- chairman, and made Greenwav-road echool lobo a boys' school, it would necessarily follow that denominational schools would suff•r more or less, because the Board would have to draw from these schools. Mr Beckett then entered into some details as to cost, 6c.— Father Fennelly contended that it would not take the enor- mous expense Mr. Beckett bad mentioned.—Mr. Beckett said he should like to be allowed to proceed with his re- marks without interreption•—Father Fennelly : We may atop here until morning.—Mr. Beckett I think not—Father Fennelly : You are stating what is not the fact you know.-- Mr. Beckett said he was assuming that the school had 2-e-Ce boys, and the greater the number of scholars the more fa- vourable was his argument to the school.—The Chairman: r said Mr. Beckett was besing his remarks upon supposition, but he ought to be allowed to make his remarks.—Mr- Beckett said he was simply giving certain figures to work upon. Tie admit only standard 3 only would also incur an Additional expense. He was more inclined to go in for pre- fiding for infants. He thought accommodation for infants was wasted. especially in Grtenway-road district, where there was only the Newtown Infant School, with a certified accommodation of 15111. It was too mach to expect infants to go down qreen way-road to the Denomina- tional Schools In town, especially infante under five years of age. He suggested thet the Board should convert one of the class-rooms into an infant echoed for the present. Ha thought this wow Id help them materially. He assumed that £lO would cover the expense that would be incurred there. They might reckon on getting 60 infants into that school, and at 2d per week for 44 weeks school fees would amount to £22. Calculating 50 passes at lOs each, although the i average for the United Kingdom was 14s 6J, gave £25 ' showing a total revenue of £47. He thought this would be 1 the best course for the Board to pursue as the present staff would be able to work the infanta and standards- cue and two, and letting standard three go to other schools. If it was necessary he would move that.—Dr. McDougall agreed with the Chairman that it would be an advantage to have an interview with Her Majesty? a In- spector. because afterwards the consent of the Education Department would be a mere formality. —Mr. linison thought that they ought to have a definite scheme to lay before H.M. Inspector. He should like to know why they should stop the discussion at standard three. If this scheme of re-arrangement had any merit in it at all its merit lay in this, that the children would not' be limited to any particular standard. They would be able to take them up to the higher standards, and he thought that would be a distinct advantage. Financially Mr. Beckett'& was the only scheme which held the field. He did not pro- fess to stand there lo defend the interests of any denomina- tion ; be was prepared to look at the question purely from a ratepayers, point of view. Mr. Beckett's was a most admir- able scheme, but at the some time he did not think it would be wise to come to a decision without the consent of Her Majesty's Inspector.—The Chairman said Mr. Beckett hadt assumed that if the Board began teaching the higher standard in the Board School the ratepayers would be involved in Considerable loss. To answer that assumption he had only, to refer him to the denominational schools of the men that teach all the higher standards, and were able to make these schools self-sustaining. (Mr. Beckett : Question ), Did Mr. Beckett mean to imply that the Beard were not capable of making these schools as efficient in the higher standards as the denominational menswears were. (Father Fenneny e I should think we ought.) Anything could be proved upon assumed figures, and Mr. Beckett did assume that so many and no much would cease in. The fact was proved by the results achieved by the work of the denominational schools. He was at the same opinion as Father remelts,* . that the only possible way to make Greenway-road Schools self-supporting was to deal with them in exactly the same way as the denominational schools of the town were dealt with. The Chairman concluded by moving a. resoletion that Her Majesty's Inspector be invited to meet the Board to confer as. to the beat mode of utilizing the certified accommodation for educational parposes.—The motion was seconded by Dr. McDougall.— Mr. Beckett said it was evident to him that the chairman felt very strongly on this matter. Ho had seen that through- out the committee meetings. He laid particular stress upon the assumptions that he (Mr. Beckett) gave. Of coarsest was not possible for him to give exact figures because be did not know how many scholars might go into Greenwar- road School, but he had assumed upon the best and most favourable basis. With regard to denominational schools paying their way the chairman did not know much of that subject. Take the Wesleyan schools, for instance, which had very high fees in the upper standards, fees as high as sixpence. At Greenway-road School 31 was paid, and other schools In the same way, In addition to which the ratepayers had to mete up the fees in case of being short in revenue to cover the expenses. In denominational schools stationery was not found for the scholars free, whereas tbe ratepayers in the Board schools found stationery free. The expenees in Board schools were heavy in comparison with other schools. He thought that was a sufficient reply to the chairman.—Father Fennell:z:. But don't they pay their way, Mr Beckett ?—Mr Beckett did not reply to the goes- tian.—Mr Imison remarked that denominatic nal schools re- geived a lot of sabscriptions.—Dr McDougall said board schools could never compete. with denominational schools that_were well managed. There was always a disposition on the part of parents to eend the children to the school with which they were connected in religion. It was how- ever, the duty of the Board to make the best of the schools they had.—Mr. Imison said Mr Beckett', assumption was justified if the Board were going to conduct their school& in the same way as the denominational schools. The motion was carried, and the meeting conclualed. ......—....---

div.p: CANAL BOAT CHILDREN.

The Clerk read a letter from Mr. Kynnersle".a, Her Ma- jesty's Inspector of Schools, who said he was directed by the Department to inquire what steps the Board had taken to carry out the Elementary Education Act with special reference to canal children under the Act of 1884.—The Chairman observed that the visitors had been getting the boat children into school as well as .they could. Mr. Beckett : Is there some reason to doubt that proper steps have not been taken.— The Clerk replied that a similar inquiry was being made of all school boards.—Mr Imison suggested the letter should be referred to the School Attendance Committee, so that they could formulate a reply.—Dr McDougall remarked that the children of boat people who lived in the town were dealt with in the same way as the obildren of other parents. The difficulty lay in dealing with those people who, although their boats were registered in Runcorn, had no habitation there. It was to the children of such parents that Mr Kynnersley no doubt referred to.—Mr Unison's sug- gaetion was agreed to. INSPECTOR'S REPORTS. The Clerk read the following reports of H.M. Inspector with regard to the recent examinations : RUNC3aN GREW:MAY-MAD Zicaam,—lfixed School : The junior school has made great progress. The children are in good order, and do very well in writing and arith- metic. Reading is lees satisfartory. Needlework excellent. Grammar good.—Gicls' School : The girls' school has made creditable progress during the year. It is now in good order, and on the whole does well in the elementary subject. There is weakness in the arithmetic of the second standard. and the first class is not good in this subject, Reading and writing are satisfactory, and the paper work is done in good style. Grammar is fair only. Needlework excellent. Berth% Smith passed in histmy and geography, and Blanche

div.p: WAREING TON TOWN COUNCIL. A monthly meeting of this Council was held at the Town Hall on Tuesday evening. There were present the Mayor (Alderman Pickmere) presiding; Alder- man Burgess. Holmes, Davies, Sutton, and Webster • Councillors Greening, J. Pierpoint. Dixon, Dakin, F. A. Roberts, Francomb, Fleming, Greenall, Jolley, Hutchinson, H. Roberts, W. Pierpoint, Marsh, and ' Wright; Messrs. Brook (town clerk), Whittle (deputy towu clerk), Chorley (borough treasurer), and Longdin (borough surveyor). THE JUBILEE VOTE TO TEE MANOR- The MAYOR Sala be had much pleasure in announcing , that the amount of £.50 which the Council voted to him to I meet the expenses ot the jubilee would not be required. They had managed without it, and had a small balance over, which he thought bad been very wisely apportioned to two or three objects in the town which rtquired a little assist- ance. It was a very small amount he was sorry to say, but still it was something. He was obliged to them for their vote.

SANEEY.STREET ON SUNDAY EVENINGS. The MAVOIL moved, and Couecillor JOLLEY seconded, the adoption of the minutes of the Watch Committee, which contained nothing of note. Councillor Dixox asked if there was any objection to giving notice teat people should not stand on the parapets in the streets? On Sunday night last he had a walk along Sankey-street between seven and eight o'clock, and he found that the parapet was filled with people standing upon It. In other towns they found notices put up that people were not to stand on the parapets. The MAYOR said as they had had several cases brought before the magistrates, he was in hopes that what Coon. Dixon referred to would have been put a stop to. Attention should, however, be given to it. The minutes were then confirmed. FINANCE COMMITTEE. The minutes of this committee, which contained only orders for payments of Accounts, were confirmed on the motion of Alderman Hotmes, seconded by Councillor GREENING. STREET IMPROVEMENT AND LIGHTING COMMITTEE. The minutes of this committee contained the following : That the plans of the foilowieg buildings be approved : Five houses in Wash-lane, for Mr. F. Carlisle ; stable and store in Church-street, for Mr. Morris; five houses in Win- marleigh-street, for Mr. H. Milling; five houses in Kauts- ford-road, Latchford, for Mr. William Eddowes ; six houses in Orford-lane, for Mr. J. Moucfield ; that a strip of land in Knuteford-road be purchased of Mr Joseph Hall upon the following tams :-1. 6s 83 per square yard (the area taken to be agreed upon between the Borough Surveyor and Mr. Owen. 2. The Corporation to remove the present gates and stumps back to the proposed line of frontage. 3. The Corporation to supply an unclimbeble iron fencing,and fix it, painted, on the new line of frontage; the iron rails to be similar to those fix,,cl by Mr. Hall opposite his cottages in Thelwall-lane. 4. All the old wood in the present fenc- ing to remain Oat proeerty of Mr Hall, and to be pat upon his premises where directed. 5. The purchase money to be paid soon the Corporation taking possession of the land. Councillor GREENING, in moving the confirmation of the minutes, referred to the proposed purchase of land in Knots- ford-road, and said this was a very desirable purchase and would lead to an improvement in the road. Councillor F. A. Homers seconded the adoption of the minutes, which was agreed to. SANITARY COMMITTEE: THE LONGFORD WORKS. The minutes of the Sanitary Committee contained as fol- lows :—That the resignation of Miss Euphemia BOSS, the matron of the Infectious Diseases Hospital, be accepted, she having obtaived the appointment of lady superintendent of the Monsale Fever firepital, Manchester. The committee in accepting the resignation, congratulate Miss Ross on her appointment, and record their entire satisfaction with the way in which she has discharged her duties since her ap- pointment in May, 1885.—That the tender of Messrs. J. and J. Horsetield, of Dewsbury, for the supply of a tank, for the storage of excreta at Longford Depot, 301 t. by Sit. 8.m., for £4B 10-e be accepted. Alderman BURGESS moved the confirmation of the minutes. Referring to the resignation of Miss Ross, he said the appointment she had received at Monsale 7ever Hos- pital was a matter upon which she might very swell be con- gratuiated. He thought it showed very cleegy that they had had a nurse in their institution very well serially of the place, and he hoped they should have in hee Aaccemor a person squally competent. (Hear, hear). Alderman SUTTON seconcled• Councillor Inicne said be roes to object to the porchase f the tank for the storage of excreta on the ground that the h airman of the committee Some time ago told them that bey had got plent sufficient for the radetafeCtere Of ail the excreta that went to tee Longford work& This tank teas required because of the breakdown which took place some time ago, and he was sorry Alderman Sutton had not given them more information than what he did at a previous meet- ing as to the breakdown, for if he had some of them might be able to use some strong language. The machinery at 15ngiord rail So slowly that they ought not to have a breakdown once in twenty years, and he was sure if pro- per attention had been paid to the machinery they would not have had teat breakdown. The MAYOR asked Alderman Burgess if he wished to reply to Councillor Dixon's remarks. Alderman Burgess replied that he did not. The minutes were then confirmed. PAVING AND SEWERAGE CO-AVITTEE.—FLOODING OF cELLARS AT LATCHFORD. The Paving and Sewerage Committee recommended that I a sewer be laid in St. Mary's-street, Latchford. That the tender of the Warrington Slate Company, Limited, for the supply of 10.000 blue bricks, at 445 63, delivered at the yard, Friars' Green, be accepted. Alderman DAVIES, in moving the cenfirrnation of the minutes, mentioned that they had now got their recently- purchased steam real roller at work. It was doing very good work at that time on Wilderspool Causeway, and he believed the committee had been congratulated by those who had driven over the road that it was almost like driv- ing over a bowling green. He was also glad to say that this work was being done at a considerable reduction of cost

to the town. The MAYOR hoped that the roller would be brought somewhere In the Peighboarheed 91 the Old Warps where it was sadly wanted. Councillor W. PIE2POINT said tleere Waa a he* sewer be- ing laid in Latchford at a considerable expense to the borough. There were cellars in Latchford which were sometimes flooded to a considerable depth, and along with the water was carried in an amount of sewage and other poisonous matter. He hoped, therefore, that the attention of the Paving and Sewerage Committee would be given to that matter in crder to see if some means could not be pclopted whereby the cellars could be drained into the new

levier. Mclennan DAVIES was glad Councillor Pierpoint had called attention to that matter. They had some very filthy water from the tanneries at that end of the borough which communicated with their sewers, but he did not think Councillor Pierpoint's works communicated with them. Councillor W. PIERFOINT : No, not at all. Alderman DAVIES said this stuff from the tanneries, he dare say, impeded the working of the sewers, but the &mg); Surveyor would do his best to remedy what Councillor Pierptint complained of. The minutes were then confirmed. THE FREE LIBRARY QtrESTION. The minutes of the Museum Library and Arts Commit- tee contained the following return :—Visitors to the Museum, 2,148, increase 37 per cent. compared with July, 1886; Books issued in reading room, 1,430, increase 27 per cent. cempared with July, 1883; Books issued in lending library, 1,418, increase 3 per cent. compared with July,

Alderman WansTaa moved, and Councillor GREENALL seconded, the confirmation of the minutes. Councillor F. A. ROBERTS said he wished for the infor- mation of the Council to ash a question of Alderman Web. liter of which he bad given him private notice. Ho was anxious to know whether the Library C minium are taking a legal course in using as a subscription library a free library supported by the rates; and also whether the Com- mittee could point out the section cf the Act which autho- rised them to thus put one ratepayer on a different footing

to another. Alderman WEBSTER, said Councillor Roberts had very courteously given him notice of his intention to ask those questions, and that had enabled him (Alderman Webster) to consult the Town Clerk as to the proper answer that should be returned. With regard to the questions, although there were two, they both pointed to one thing, and it was quite unnecessary to separate one from another. One an- swer would suffice without going into details, and he could only say that the Library Committee is not taking any ille- gal course in the mode in which it is now managing the library. The mientes of the committee were then confirmed. SCHOOL ATTENDANCE COMMITTEE. This Committee's minutes contained the following Report of the inspector that 112 cases had been inquired into by the Boord of Guardians, and school fees allowed in 108 cases for 205 children. That 22 cases had been taken before the magistrates, and flues inflicted in 18 cases, 2 sent to the ship' and 1 ordered to be whipped. Note: 35 cases were brought before the Committee, and dealt with." On the motion of Alderman WEBSTER, seconded by Councillor FLSMING, the minutes were passed. CEMETERY COMMITTEE. The minutes of the Cemetery Committee contained the following:—Reoort of the registrar, from which it appeved that the interments for the past four weeks were :—Adults, 28; minors, 48; and stillborn and premature, 11; and for the corresponding period last year, :—Adults, 31; minors, 36; stillborn and premature. 7. Note.—The receipts for the past weeks were £62 16s Bd, and for the corresponding period last year. £57 lOs 9d. On the motion of Councillor JOLLEY, seconded by Conn- tiller FLEMING, the minutes were adopted. THE SANKEY-STREET WALL—TEE REMOVAL SCHEME AGAIN DEFEAT. The minutes of the Town Hall, Park, and Baths Com- mittee contained the following :—Report of the bathkeePer, from which it appeared that the income from the baths for the past four weeks was £5l 9s 11d, and for the correspond- ing period last year, £42 13s 81. That William Ashten be appointed park-keeper, at 21s per week. That the sum of be voted for the purchase of hyacinths and other bulbs. That the wall in front of the Town Ball be removed, and a suitable pal:sang substituted in lieu thereof, in accordance with the plan now submitted and approved, at an estimated cost of £4OO.

The Ma.vott moved, and Councillor J. PISRPOiNT. seconded, the adoption of minutes. The MAYon, referring to the minute with regard to the removal of the watt in front of the Town Hall, said be thought it must have struck anyone who was an inhabitant of the town that a building like the Town Hall ought to be open to public view. (Hear, hear.) Lt., certainly thought that all public offices should be easy of approach and access to the public, who shou'd be able to have a view of them as they went about their daily avocations, if they liked to turn their heads in that direction. They all knew that a person passing along Sankey-street could not obtain a view of the Town Hall or grounds, owing to the unsightly wall at the front; and he had for many yeas been of opinion, in fact ever since they had a Town Hall, that it would be a capital thing to remove the wall and open the place out to the street. He had spoken to a great mane inhabitants not connected with the Corporation—to men who were rate- pavers—and there was not a single dissentient that the re- moval of the wall would be a great improvement as well as a relief to the overpressure of which Councillor Dixon com- plained as existing in Sankey-street. Councillor Durosr.-1 do not think there is over-pres-

sure. The Mayon, continuing, said that people would prob- aOly have a walk in front of the Town Hall if the wall was removed, instead of stanaing about the street to the annoyance of Councillor Dixon. With reference to the cost, he might be told that they had not estimated for the amount in the estimates, but surely the Corporation of Warrington could have credit to the extent ofe,g4oo. (Hear, hear.) There were stays and means cf getting the money it they required it, and the wall could be taken down any time they liked to say it should be removed. fie sheuld certainly vote for its removal, and that the work be done in a proper and substantial manner, as the alteration would be an orna- ment to the town generally. They bad now a first-class plan before them, and he hoped there would be a unanimous vote on the question. (Hear, bear.) Alderman DAVIES moved an amendment "That the minutes of the Committee be confirmed with the exception of the resolution of the 25th August propasing that the wall in front of the Town Hall be removed, and a suitable palisading substituted in lieu thereof, in accordance witht the plan now submitted and approved, at an estimated COSO of £400." He rematked that he was not present at th meeting of the Committee, as he was not a member of it but he understood that the vote on the question was not a unanimous one. (Hear, hear.) One gentleman made a speech very much against the removal of the wall, and yet in an extraordinary faehion he voted for its removal. That was, however, a matter of little moment. That Town Hall was almost of heroic character compared with other build jugs in Warrington, and f they pat up a fenee, as be sew Indicated by the minutes it would be very much like having a brass knocker to a pigcote door. (Laughter.) They ap- peared to be speaking as if the public had not free access to the whole of the buildings and grounds. Anyone who wished to go into the grounds was not debarred from doing so, either by day or night, and he had ample opportunity not only of seeing the Town Hall but the enclosures, which were very ;much improved by having a sunk fence and a grass plot presented to the view. At the present time they had a very black sheet before them as to money they would be required to pay. That was a matter that was well weighed over by the Paring and Sewerage Committee when they suggested the purchase of the steam roller, and they proposed to spend half the money one half year and tbe other half during another half year to • enable them to keep within the estimates. lie hoped Alder- man Burgess would not be angry when he said that they would have to spend a great deal more money at Longford. (Hear, hear.) They could not shut their eyes to that fact, and it was no reflection on the committee to say that more money would be required, and then the works would be a success. They had several thousands of pounds to spend there in duplicate machinery. ("Oh, oh," and a Member :" Oh Moses.") Well, Moses was a very goad sanitary man. (Laughter, and a Member : Bat he did not. use machinery). Bui, the Moses of this day had to do so They had also to pay a thousand a year for the money they had overspent is Bridge-street. And a matter that was in the future was the coming into force of the Rivers Pollu- tion Act, and with regard to that they knew that they were perhaps as badly situated as any town in Lancashire, because unfortunately their sewage was not being sent into the river only at one point. He thought, therefore, with these things before them they ought to be very careful and not spend £4OO that was not in the estimates over a thing that was not worth it. (Hear, hear). Councillor BOi.TON seconded the amendment. He would have been very glad, he said, to have seen the wall removed lithe Jubilee Commit-ee would have found the funds, but he did not think it was right because the Jubilee Commit- tee could not get the money out of the people of Warring- ton that they ehould COM and &crew it out of Ole shop- tWperS afel Ogler ratepayer. ;the rate's next year he understood would be as much as they were at present, and they were now higher than ever before. ("No, no.') Well, he thought they were considering the increase of propetty there had been, but it seemed to him tbat the rate.; were like the gas hills •, the gas was cheaper, but the bills were heaver. (Hear, bear, and laughter.) There was no doubt they were paying more mance, in the end. (Hear, hear.) This was not the time to carry out that scheme. Let them wait till Longferd paid the £3,000 a year towards the relief of the rates. (Laughter.) They had been told that the gas works would lessen the rates, but he found that these things were never done. (Laughter). Councillor JOLLEY said, as a member, not only of the Town Hall and Parks Commitee, but also of the Jubilee Committee, he would support the resolution of the Mayor. He thought that the public expression which had been ; given in that reom, when they were told that the Jubilee ' committee would spend any surplus money in taking down flee wall, was a guarantee that tha public wished the wall taken dowh. (Hear, hear.) He was surprised to hear Aldermen Davies speak as he had done, and he thought there was some feeling beyond the £lOO. The public wished the wall pulled down. (" No, no.") Yes, they did. ("No, no.") „Yes, and the Jubilee Committee were authorized to spend money in pulling down the wall, and the ratepayers were desirous to have it down. He would supeort the resolution with all the energy he possibly could, for be thought the wall was a disgrace and a nuis- ance to the town of Warrington. Councillor JOHN Pintootsio ale() supported the resolution. As to the question of money, he hoped that a decision would be arrived at,whereby the matter would be placed in the hands of a competent person, and one who could wait a short time for his money. Alderman Devies was the means, in a ' great measure of the Council going to that hall. Surely be was not ashamed of it. (Hear. hear.) It was a hand- some building, and well worthy of a view from any person passing it in Sankey-street; bat was there a single building of note in any town hidden by a blank wall at least ten or twelve feet high, the same as it was ? Why they should appear to be so odd and stubborn in beautifyino their town he really could not 'understand, and he would, therefore, support the resolution that the plan should be carried out. (Hear, hear.) Alderman itlatos, in supporting the Intendment, said he did so on financial grounds, as be thought it was an expense which it was not necessary to incur. Councillor Jolley had said that at a large meeting which was held in that hall the people present all thought it was a necessity that the wall should come down ; but it should be borne in mind that they gave no sanction for any money being taken out of the rates to pay for the taking of it down. There was no quesiion that they had before them a large increase of expenditure an capital account. Alderman Davies had referred to an eXpenditare likely to be incurred in connec- tion with Longford works, and be could tell them that there was another Longford works which weuld require a 'large amount on capital expenditure in the next two years or so. Looking at all these things he did hope they would let luxuries of that sort stand aside, end not spend money except in the face of absolute necessity. (Hear, hear.) Alderman SITTTOII said he thought it was a pity that the question should be treated as it was by some members of the Council because, as they saw, it was a fact that the great majority of the inhabitants of the town were in favor of the wall being pulled down. Some members of the Council had on every occasion tried to make them under- stand the necessity for open spaces in the borough—(hear, Lear)—but here they had got a large portion of ground in the centre of the town which was at present perfectly use- less. (Laughter, and "Quite right.") There was no one who had the privilege of enjoying that piece of ground, either for recreation or any other purpose whatever; and by nulling down the wall they might do away with a good deal of the evil complained of by Counciller Dixon. It did really seem, as bad been said, that there was something more than the expense of taking down the wall, but he did not know what it was. (Hear, hear.) Councillor Menai, in supporting the resolution, said he did not think it was only the spending of £4OO which some gentlemen of tae Council objected to, for it was no such thing. More than one of those who opposed the proposal thought very little indeed about spending so many thousands and for purposes ot much less interest to the public c,f Warrington; but that was only an excuse. Had a certain building on the opposite side of the street been at Hull— (hear, hear, and laughter)—and the beautifel fouetain promised by Sir Gilbert Greenall been with it, he thought they would have heard very little about the money, and there would not have been the least trouble. tLaughter, and hear, hear.) Councillor DIXON, in supporting the amendment, said it 'as not more than four or five hours since he bad been speaking to a manufacturer, who informed him that their works were being carried on without any margin of profit. About three weeks or a fortnight ago a person repotted to him that there was a firm in town which generally paid an average dividend, but this year there would be nothing for them. Under these circumstances he thought it was the duty of all interested in the borough to strive by all the means in their power to keep the rates down. He was quite sure that if they went to manutacturers at the present time, one and all would tell them that the rates were heavier in proportion to what they were earning. (Hear,
"was

. - hear.) Alderman RundEss said the members of the Council had been challenged more than once that night with having something in the background. He was free to confess be had something in the background, and it was this, that it any gentleman, or any number of gentlemen combined, would subscribe the money necessary for the removal of the wall he would not take it from their hands. He looked upon the proposed removal of the wall as a piece of van- dalism. The Town Hall was in a retired condition, and it was at the same time an ornament. Do what they were asked to do with the £4OO and they would destroy the re- tiremeat and privacy that were so valuable in this instance; and they would do what had been suggesttd by some of , their friends, make the place into a playground for cbil.

l. dren. They had a recreation Ground already, and the wall did net interfere with it. The directors of one of their large railway companies, upon a visit to this town some time ago, expressed great admiration of the privacy of the Town Hall 'at Warrington, and they were gentlemen who came from a town which possessed one of the most magnificent Town Halls in the whole of the kingdom, and one that was more exposed than most Town Halls, and they expressed the wish that their Town Hall, magnidcent as it was, could be of the same character as the one at Werrlugton with regard to retirement. Alderman Surroer : Oh, they don't understand it. (Laugh- ter.) The MAYOR: Where is the Town Hall you speak of? Alderman BURGESS: It is no secret. It is the Manchester Town Hall, and the directors were the directors of the Man- chester, Sheffield, and Lincolnshire Railway. I hope we shall have the sense to leave this Town Hall where it is. It will serve for discussion another time. 'the MAYOR: It seems to be a favourite discussien. Alderman HARRISON said he waa surprised when he found Alderman Davies opposing, as he had a right to do, what would be a valuable and an unmistakeable improve- meet to the building in which ne had taken so lively an interest. He would ask whether any man in his senses would think of supporting the erection of a Town Hall and• build at the front a big ugly wall of ten feet or twelve feet? Talk about vandalism, it existed at the present time in the present wall. (Hear, hear.) Remove the wall, and the vandalism disappeared altogether. (Hear, hear.) What man in his senses would ever think of supporting the re- tention of a wall in front of a building that was certainly a credit to Warrington, and a building that would answer their purpose as a Town Hall Ice many years to come. He most confess that he felt almost ashamed of the Warring- ton Town Council is attempting to oppose such a moderate expenditure of money for so palpable and great an advan- tage. They must remember that this was supposed to be a Jubilee effering to her Majesty. The Town Council up to the present time had not contributed anything towards the Jubilee of her Majesty. He thought they had been exces- sively shabbv—(" No, no ")—whilst other towns had spent considerable sums to demonstrate their loyalty to their Sovereign, in Warrington as far as the Town Coun- cil was concerned, they had grade no movement at all: If the wall were removed not only would it be a delight to the whole of the inhabitants, but it would give them what they were unjustly and practically excluded from using at the present time when they came into the enclosure, where they found a lot of pillars and chains. What was the meaning of it? It was a moral prohibition against anyone l entering within the precincts of the wall. They had no right to do so, as the place belonged to the public. It was a recreation ground, and the public ought to have the freest l possible access to it. (Hear, hear.) Alderman DAVIES (referring to a plan).—The fence pro- posed will be harder to get over than the stumps. Alderman HARRISON would make a proper entrance to the enclosure He felt sorry that any controversy ,of this kind should have been raised on a question of such a simple character—a trumpery sum of £4OO, whioh would cost a more little than a halfpenny in the £. Councillor IL ROBERTS said that having opposed the proposal of the Committee he would not be doing justice to himself if he gave a silent vote. The estimate of £4OO did not include the whole of the cost that would be incurred if th 3 wall was taken down, and that the Committee were wel, aware of. He asked the question in Committee at the last meeting, whether the £4OO included anything more than the taking down of the wall and the erection of the palisad- , log, and he was told it did not. What were they going to de with the land when they had taken the wall down? If It was to be made of use for public purposes it most be laid nut in a suitable manner, and that meant another £4OO. ("Nonsense.") Councillor JOLLEY.—You know that our own staff can do what we want here. £4OO is all we intend to spend. Councillor H. ROBERTS said he did not know anything of the sort, and he did not believe in the possibility of laying out the ground without considerable extra cost, and he ob- jected on principle to the mortgaging of the rates of another year to carry out the work of the present year. There was year consideration. They proposed to give up a portion of the land to the street. He said they had no right to do anything of the kind, and he would take means to have the legal question decided as to the right of the Town Council to appropriate recreation ground for public purposes. As this was a fad, and nothing more than a fad, he objected to it altogether, and to its being suggested that there were ulterior motives operating on members of the Council. (Hear, bear.) As long as the baths were in their present disgraceful condition be would object to any expenditure which was not a positive necessity. Councillor Joule PIERPOINT : I shall object to new baths. (Laughter.) Councillor H. ROBELTS : This is a matter from which no ona Will ruff.Pr if the wall remains as it is for 20 years. (Hear, hear.) The MAYOR wet Orly the question of an ulterior ob- ject had been brought forward. He could say on his own behalf, and on behalf of the members cf the Committee, that they had no ulterior object in view; their only object was to improve the front of the Town Hall. (Hear, hear.) Councillor JOLLEY : The general public require the altera- tion. Alderman DAVIES : I honour all who will vote against me in this matter, as I hope they will honour those who vote with me. I was surprised to hear that anyone had ulterior views. The Mayon : I think that question ought to have been left out. The voting was then proceeded with. and resulted as follows : For the amendment—Aldermen Holmes, Burgess, Davies, Webster, Councillors F. A. Roberts, Dakin, Greening, W. Pierpoint, Fleming, Bolton, Dixon, and H. Roberts, 12. Against the amendment—Alderman Harrison and Sut- ton, Councillors John Pierpoint, Marsh, Hutchinson, Jolley, Greenall, Fran comb, Wright. and the Mayor, 10. The MAYOR therefore declared the amendment carried by 12 to 10 votes. The minutes were then confirmed, with the exeeption of the one referring to the removal of the wall. Councillor JOLLEY : All right. There is plenty of time. The work will be carried out yet. PRICES.

The Gas Committee met on the 29th July, when it was teeolved "That the following tenders for the supply of coal and cannel for the nest twelve months be accepted : Whitecross Company, Limited, 3,000 tons of cancel; John Brown and Co., 3,500 tons of coal: Blainscough Hall, 3,500 tons of coal; Pearson and Knowles, 3,000 tons of coal ; Wigan Coal and Iron Co., 3,000 tees of coal ; Mess Hall, 3,000 tons of coal; Garwood Hall, 2,000 tons of cot!; total, 21,000 tons.—At a meeting held on the sth August, the average illuminating power of the gas during the fortnight , ended sth August was reported to be equal to 17 candles, and during the fortnight ended 19th August, 18 candles at both works. Alderman limas moved, and Alderman WEBSTER se- conded the confirmation of the minutes. Councillor BOLTON asked why the prices were not pub- lished for the contracts for coat and cannel. He believed that a resolution had been passed to the effect that the prices of accepted contracts should be published, and he did not see why that should now be omitted. Councillor H. ROBERTS said that he could not understand the action of the Gas Committee in deliberately setting aside the order of the Council in this matter. It might be all very well to say that in the interests of the contractors the prices were kept secret, but it was certainly not in the Interests of the public that the prices should be hidden, and it was not fair to other contractors that the contracts for certain things should be published, and that in a case like this, where there was a large sum of money involved, they should not be published. Contractors might prefer that their prices should be kept secret, but they must consider what was due to the public. It having been decided that the prices of all contraCte, 'should be pmblished, it was most unfair on the part of the Gas Committee to take the procee- dings they had done. They had no right to do it with- out getting the Council to cancel the resolution previously passed. Alderman Svrrox said that he had sufficient confidence in the Gas Committee to think that they would publish all that was necessary and deairable. He did not think that they would accept any contract unless it was to their ad- vantage to do so, and he did not think it was at all neces- sary that in all cases the prices should be published. Councillor Whin= said that the matter was very care- fully weighed over and the Committee CAM to the conclu- sion that they were serving the best interests of the rate- payers in not publishing the prices. He thought that the sooner the resolution referred to was rescinded, the better it would be for the interests of the Corporation. Alderman HARRISON said that as a member of the Gas Committee he was satisfied that whatever the Committee had done with reference to these contracts had been done in the interests of the public. If Mr. Roberts felt himself ag- grieved. let him move a vote or censure, and let the Gas Committee be superseded by same one more competent. Councillor Dixon: I would be glad— Councillor BOLTON: I asked why they have not been published, and I have had no answer to satisfy me. Alderman Houerns said that the Committee considered that it was in the interests of the Council, and of the rate- payers that the prices should not be published. He had a list of prices which any member whe wished to could see. They were also in the minute bock, which any member could see. The price was a little lees than what was paid lest year, and they believed that they had got the best con- tract. The minutes were then adopted. MARKETS C03131/TIEE. A REMARKABLE WOMAN. Occasionally cases are heard of in which members of the gentler sex have voluntarily adopted the garb and manners a the sterner portion of human- ity, and there have been instances Of women who have earned their living at arduous occupations, and who have for years been supposed to be men. Women in the guise of men have even fought for their country and have fought bravely, too. There have been, of course, other cases in which females have donned men's attire in a freak or have used it for a short period as a means to attaining a definite end in view, but these are not cases to be classed in the same category with those of persons who have voluntarily, and for a b,ng continued time cast off their women's clothes, and with the adoption of male attire have also adopted the rough and ready work to which men in some walks of life are accustomed to. All that was mortal of a woman of this class was on Monday laid under the sod in the churchyard at , Great Sankey. Harriet Taylor, better known in Warrington and for miles around as "Happy Ned," was for a considerable portion of her life supposed by the generality of the people whom she lived among to be a man, and a pretty strong and robust specimen of the race. She was at the time of her death, which took place last week after a long illness, fifty-six years old, and she is credited with having passed through numerous and stirring adventures. If all that is said about her past career is true, it has indeed been a remarkable one. On several ()c- -essions she has appeared at the borough polioe court, in con6equence of a fondness for Warrington ale, and she first made her appearance before "their worships" at the Sessions House, in Irlam-street, in the year 1872, when it was insinuated against her that she had been intoxicated, and also dis- orderly, in the Eagle ancl:Child yard. The insinua- tion seems to have been well' founded, for the police books record that she was "let off" on paying the usual five shillings, and, as it was a firstoffence,the costs were included. When thus dealt with she was dressed in male attire, and was supposed to be a man. Subsequent to this date, she was charged , with similar offences at the police court, and on each occasion she was dressed in men's clothes. In 1885, however, she seems to have returned to her female dress. In that year a woman was locked up for having been drunk and disorderly on Town Hill, and the surprising 'discovery was then made that this person was no other than "Happy Ned." So complete was the change in her appearance that it I was some time before the police—and policemen usually .have keen eyes—recognised this woman as the "man" *who had been known to them' as "Happy Ned." The discovery caused some excite- ment at the moment, but since then and up to the time of her death very little has been heard of the deceased, who lived in the Narrow iVynt, off Butter- market-street. It has been stated that "Happy Ned" was also once a sailor, that she went to America, and there "saw duty" in the War of Secession, and was engaged in blockade running. Inquiries which have been mad of people who ap- pear to have had a personal knowledge of the career and characteristics of "Happy Ned," throw some doubt on the accuracy of the statement. De- ceased was away from the neighbourhood for some ' time, and it is said that when she returned she her- self gave it out that she had been as a sailor to America, and there the matter rests. That at one time she has passed off as a sailor is proved by the fact that on pne of the docu- Aleuts in the possession of the police she is described as a "farm labourer and Ballots." It is perfectly true that for some tint§ sho main- tained herself as a navvy, and worked as hard as any of the rough-banded sons of toil with whom she was associated, and she has also worked as a farm labourer. It is said that she worked among the navvies when the Cheshire Lines Railway was laid. "Happy Ned" was about Sit. 6in, in height, usually wore a cap, smoked a short " catty" pipe, and was among the other navvies considered "a jolly good fellow." Indeed he—or rather she—ap- pears to have been of a very lively temperament, Her selection of an arduous life did not make her morose. She ronglied it merrily, and so exuberant were her spirits as to gain for her the name by which she was sd well known. Even under what would usually be considered very depressing cir- cumstances, she maintained, her light-heartedness, and when temporarily de7F)rived of her liberty she would sing 'gaily while in durance vile. She wag evidently one who did not meet trouble half way. The real name of this remszkable woman was Har- riet Davies, but she is said go have been married to a man named Taylor, with whom, however, she had not lived for a long period. To take the liberty of altering Shakespeare, it is fitting to say in conclu- sion : _

It is stated that Mr. Chamberlain will address his con- stituents at the end of the month. The right hon. gentle- man la resolved to keep his engagements at Manchester and Belfast. BRITISH ASSOCIATION,—The various sections of the Bri- tish Association for the Advancement of Science met on Tuesday, together with several sub-sections. In the after- noon a general committee meeting was held at Owens Col- lege. Sir Isaac Lowthian Bell and a deputation from New- castle-on-Tyne were present to invite the association to meet in that city in 1889. The association accepted the Invitation. On the motion of Caritain Sir Douglas Galton, seconded by Sir F. Abel, S.ir F. Bramwell, C.E., was appointed president of the Bath meeting, which will be held on the sth September next year. Other officers for the year were appointed. After the business of the day was over, a large number of members proceeded to Peel Park, to attend a garden party to which they were invited by Sir James Farmer, Mayor of Salford. Sir Francis de Winton spoke on "Explorations in Central Africa,", at the Free Trade Ball in the evening.--.-On Tuesday Dr. Fahlberg ex- hibited the substance, saccharine, produced from coal tar. The economic and geological sections sat together, to hear a paper by Mr. W. Tapley, of the geological survey, on the future production of the precious metals. O. n Wednesday the final meeting was held. AmOng the subjects discussed were bi-metallism and the Channel Tunnel. The amount received for tickets has enabled the Association to set apart a larger amount for grants for scientific purposes than has been given in any previous year—namely, £1,975. The Association will meet in Bath in 1888.

OPEN CHURCHES.

Sir,—lf I understand aright, the buildings erected for public prayer are for the pure worship of Almighty God, and to be in spirit and is truth. People who appropriate particular parts of a building so sit apart for worship from their poor neighbours must be of a nature very selflish or full of pride. Bringing such a feeling into the noose of prayer cannot be pure worship, therefore constittites sin. For St James in his 2nd chapter says he that hath respect of persons committath sin. In miking these few remarks I do trust the old congregation of Trinity Church, "for it may appl^ to all congregttions," will, when complete, take into consideration the responsible position they place them- selves in should they insist on any particular place or seat In the House of God, that is if thei look upon it as the House of God.—Yours truly, A FREE AND OPEN CHURCHMAN.

div.head: JUBILEE FUND.
div.p: THE JUBILEE FUND.

Sir,—l are from your paper last week that the local jubi- lee fund has been closed and that it has been decided to hand over the balance of some wounds to certain objects. It cannot be complained that there has been any undue haste to wind up this fund, but has the winding up of it not been done in a somewhat irregular fashion ? There was a large committee formed on which the various interests and different denominations and societiea of the town were represented. and I always understood that this committee was the body which had to determine in what manner the money that was raised in connection with the jubilee should be spent. It was this committee which decided in what proportions the fund was to be spent on scholars' treat, fireworks. ate., but it does aot seem that it has been at all consulted with regard to the disposal of the balance. That has been managed entirely by the small sub-committee that was appointed to see to the carrying out of the decisions of the general committee. It looks very much as if this sub- committee had usurped a power it was never intended to have. It is not difficult to imagine that a majority of the general committee might have been disposed to use the bal- ance in soma other way than that decided upon by the sub- committee. Warrington, September 6, 1887.
QUERIST.
VIE WARRINGTON CiERVIAN CLASS.

- Sir.—rhe reading of " Clifford Dies " letter in your last issue respecting the Warrington German Class reminded me of a forcible illustration of the pOsition Englishmen take respecting foreign languages. I was dining in a Freoch Restaurant on ens occasion when four young men entered in company. One was unmistakably French, the second of doutdful nationality, and the two others rank John Bulls. The Orst and second gave their orders in a businest-like style, and then conversed together in French. The two others consulted the Carte, turned it upside down, and round about, but could make nothing of it. Their great anxiety was for a b Atte of Bass's beer, but they could net make the waiter understand what they wanted. Meanwhile their coin- panions got their orders executed and proceeded leisurely with their dinners. Course succeeded course with them but the two pronounced Englishmen could get nothing to eat. It transpired that the doubtful gentleman was English, the Frenchman spoke his native tongue only; and the other Britons spoke Ence,lish only. The French-speaking English- men kept up a conversation with his French friend, and paid no attention to his countrymen, who fared very badly. One of the Englishmen got very uneasy, and at last testily remarked to his donble.tong.ned friend " Look here : why does not your friend learn English ?" Just like an Eng- lishman, thought I. To learn French had evidently never entered this Englishman's head ; the idea of it was, doubt- less, ridiculous.— Your, &c. PROGRESS.

THE INTERCEPTING DEPOTS. Bir,—Consictering the great complaints which have been made of the stench arising from these depots, and the amount of sickness which now exists in some parts of the town, and the widespread disagreeable smell in the dwell- ines and shops in the c mtre of the town, it is astonishing that at the Council meeting on Tuesday night last not one member of it except Mr. Councillor Dixon dared raise his voice, when asked by the Mayor to do so, against the sicken- ing smell the iebabitants in the vicinity of these depots have to eedure, and the foreshadowed large additional expendi- ture that the town is going to be put to in connection with these hot beds of diseases; when only a few months ago, as it were, they were all driven, at a cost of about £l5 of the ratepayers' money, to witness what was then said a comple- tion of a grand sanitary scheme which was to serve War- rington withoet any further expenditure for the next 20 years, Mr. Alderman Davies's remarks that many more thousands of pouvids will be wanted for duplicate ma- chinery, &c., before these depots can be made a success should open the eyes of the ratepayers of the town. I won- der if they know that already this Longford job and its effnections bavecost the town something like £20,000? For what? For works which everybody complains of, and in time will have to be condemned. I may, sir, have to trouble you next week eon the expenditure in connection with these places; but in the meantime let me ask where the excreta that could not be taken in at Longford has gone to? I am told it has been pitched down the sewers in the small hours of the morning, and people in the town have had to endure the stench, and the police on duty have had to go home ill from the effects of it, expressing a desire to be on day duty rather than night. I hesitate be believe thia. It is a fact that the rinsing of the pails is sent dawn the sewers. It might also be asked where does the excreta go to which cannnot be forced up the pipes? I myself have seen 70 tube full at one time. It is well knoWn that this portion of the stuff contains the very essence of it, and it would be well to know whether it is said or given away. It might also be asked is it true that in the neighbourhood of Lvtbgoe'e-laise children have had to be taken to the fever hospital, and that a large amount of sickness exists there, all attributable to the stench arising from the depot there? And lastly. is it true that in Palmyra-square, &c., the gathering vans and scent pots have to be cleared away by eight o'clock in the morning, while the hard working-man and lii family has to endure them at noonday—at dinner time? When these injustices exist, I don't wonder at the cry of the "Masses against the classes." I wish, Mr. Editor, this was an "Irish grievence ; " it would soon be settled.

THE TEMPERANCE QUESTION. Sir,—l have read with much interest "Clifford Dix's" letter on "The Temperance Question." He is quite as much concerned about the poverty and degradation around us, caused through (what some people think) intemperance as are Mr. Langham, Mr. W. Roberts or Mr. Yonge, only that his method of cure is different. "The Temperance Question " is one of the cries of the well-to-do-class; they see things are going wrong and put it all down to intemper- ance, and sometimes to Idleness and thriftlessness. Teeto- talism is then insisted on by them for the cure of the for- , mer, and vegetarianism to the thriftless, and some other thing to the idle, and so on it goes. Ido not for a moment doubt the earnestness of these peeple, but Ido object to this wholesale slander of the poor by so many well- meaning people. If We studied economics more and senti- ment less, we should see that it is the fearful economic condition of to-day that is the cause of the misery.—" Un- paid labour,"—hew many of the well-to-do class realiz3 what these two words really mean? How many realize the result of unpaid labour?--the misery, in other words, that is caused by people being underpaid. When I hear ef teetotal- ism or vegetarianism, tinder our present condition of society, I can see what it amounts to, and what its results will be. Those of us who think,.or know anything of the labour question, know that a workman's wage is regulated ac- cording to what he can subsist on (however even this in many trades is not considered, piece work being the order of the day, still further showing at what a disadvantage the worker is) so that when he is made teetotal and vegetarian, down will go his wages to that limit. While a feW com- paratively as now are teetotallers and vegetarians, they reap a little benefit, but should all the workers be of the same mind their position will be altered, for down will go their wages to the benefit of the employing class, and this is what I mean by "unpaid labour," and to ass Mr. Walter Betant's words, quoted by "Clifford Dix," there are " thousands of men and women continually occupied in miserable toil for wretched wages, who never venture to hope for any cessation or relaxation of the life sentence to which they are doomed at their birth?' What better will they be should they become teetotallers, for as it is they "are continually occupied in miserable toil," (not work) fer wretched wages?" In dealing with a question of this magnitude we must deal with the general question; the question as it aifec.ts the -whole, not individuals—which in questions of this kind people are apt to do. Before closing I must have a word or two with ''Clifford Dix." His panacea is "education, sanitary improvements, better dwellings for the poorer classes." All good; but per- mit me to draw his attention to a few facts, which, along with the labour question, has to be first settled before we can hope for an educated, healthy, and temperate people. Oxford and Cambridge, and other colleges, are monopolised by noblemen and those of the highest rank, who do not re• fuse " free education," but on the contrary, are proud of it, while at the same tune it is argued that "free education " will pauperise the people. We sit in judgment on the criminal (intemperate) and the Pauper, but what about those , who live on the devastation of the society they have pro- ' duced, for have you not the same class living on the rents ' of the poor? They have not only taken ten millions of acres of land from the people, but have also robbed the people of their schools. These are the questions we have to solve, and our .Temperance people should throw a lit- tle more energy in. this direction, so that the masses may get a fair chance in life. and when they do, they will not need to run to the public-house for comfort. I must take notice of a remark or two in your leader on the subject, without going into the question of the result of intemperance, which every one knows to be bad, and which 0 CliffOrd Dix" does not dispute. I have dwelt

sufficiently upon the cause aad remedy—but I should like to point out that when dealing with the "publican " you have a greater power than him to combat. You say—" We agree with Cliff ird Dix ' in looking to education and sanitation as aids to temperance; but we are entirely opposed to him I in thinking that it is desirable that 'there should be less interference with the publicans.' There is an enforcement of the law which provides that the offender who is drunk and disorderly shall be punished; bat from some cause or other we hear little of the provision for punishing the landlord who makes him drunk. Publicans require to be more interfered with in that and in other respects. The more they are tied down and the less mischief they will do." But what about the twenty-three members of Parlia- ment who are brewers? Do you think that it is likely that they any more than the landlord class will legislate against their own interests? Although I am not a teetotaler, lam a
