WHAT IT'S COMING TO. Sir,—You have been kind enough to allow me, at various times, to give expression to my deep concern on the ques- tion of competition. For this I thank you, as lam con- vinced that it lies at the very roots of all our troubles. Unfortunately its great significance has not made itself quite clear be the bulk of the people. There is an idea that through competition only are we enabled to make progress, that only by pitting brains against brains can we carry out the evolutionary features characteristic of human nature. We give no credit to the poet, the preacher, the musician, or the mechanic, for an innate love of his profession; each one is supposed to be guided and controlled by the desire to gain wealth, because society has laid down the law that "An empty pocket's the worst et crimes." Shall we pause soon, and ask ourselves where is it all leading us to? We have seen the preacher responding to a "call" if it led to a well-paid benefice; now we read there is a scarcity of intel- lectual men at the colleges in consequence of a more attrac- tive call to mercantile pursuits. Yet this is not the rule; the poet, the preacher, the musician, and the mechanic, hold their own wherever real excellence is put forth, but it must be excellence, as stern competition insists that mediocrity must take a back seat. It still remains that a man's best powers are put forth, nay, are fully developed, in spite of what may be their money value in the market. What we have to determine is, have these several quali- ties a money value, or are they not rather a trust, intended to be used for the benefit and advantage of the community, payment in return being in kind, and so the social theory binding the human family together in one harmonious whole, and banishing competition? Of couree no such rulea as these obtain at present, and I can fancy some of my readers having a good laugh, and saying, "And never will." Well, whatever may be in the future, there can be no mis- taking the fact that very few thoughtful men are satisfied with things as they are present. Looking ever the reports of the meetings of the British Association for the past ten years, one feature stands out very prominent, that is, that the disciples of the "dismal sciecce" have been forced to acknowledge in a round-about way that laws framed by mere theorists work badly when put in practice. Professor Schunk eays—" All human institutions piss through the some phases; they have their rise, they cul- minate, and decay. Moreover it is a natural law that what- ever develops rapidly also declines rapidly." I am not of those who think England is likely to decline rapidly, but judging from evidence coming from all quarters, that is, evidence such as Lord Derby's on agricelture and ,Stephen Mason's, M.P., on our industries, I am satisfied that other and very different modes mast be adopted, if we wish for a contirm ince of the British nation's hitherto prosperous course.

Leaving the Derby evidence for future treitment, and dealing with Mr. Mason'e, we find him saying—" Foreign competition, both at home and abroad, becomes still more and more tierce, and much of the business which formerly reached these shores is slowly but surely being transferred to other ceuntries." The usual explanation to this is, he states, "over production at home and lower wages abroad." Mr. Mason sees plainly, and, as it has been pointed out scores of times by the Socialists, that there cannot be over- production, generally speaking, so long "as we have so many unsatisfied wants, old enealor and poverty in our midst." We may have, as I have pointed out several times, a wretched syste ea of • distribution, heaps of shoes in the shoe shop, shelves full to overflowing in the clothes shop, and ragged and shoeless urchins in the street. The difficulty in the present system of distribation is to bring the would- be customer and the dealer together a little oftener. This, however, does not trouble Mr, Mason. What he. as a mer- chant and a late President of the Glasgow Chamber of Commerce, desires to see is our production increased so that we may more successfully compete with the foreigner, and to do this he suggests that we at ooce adopt what is called the double shift' or "two site of hands" mode of working. We, he save, display much skill at Oldham and elsewhere in making machinery for foreigners who ran it Is more advantage. " Tbe increase of spindles and looms on the Continent goes on apace, and the results are highly satisfactory compared with the dwindling profits in Eng- land." Mr. Mason is quite clear that the wage question is net the bugbear so often asserted, as he states, "trade is always good when wages are high:" Workmen have thought. and given expression to this opinion oft-times, bu". they are of no account, but now it is in evidence that " the wages pld to the operative bears a very small proportion to the cost of the article produced. On a pound weight of cotton yarn, costing 10d, it won't exceed lid to the operatives." Now then, what is the remedy? 'I his—" I arcs thoroughly con- vinced that the machinery must be made to do more, and run, say, from'd a.m. till 11 p.m., with two sets of bands, one leaving off at 2.0 or 2-30, and the other leaving work at 11 p.m."This, then, is the remedy for bad trade. We are to bare the Continental system introduced, from Sunday at midnight till Saturday at midnight. Life will be worth living shortly. But. says Mr. Mason—" The hours of the operatives would be thus reduced, and one half of the day practically left free for educational and social purposes, and at the same time capital invested would be rendered more profitable." With this brilliant idea commended to us, we are left in a blue. study. Mr. Mason is satisfied "it will bear the fullest investigation." I may be somewhat obtuse, but as a matter of fact, I know of a score or two of men who are passing a life of enforced idleness. If to encourage trade it is necessary to work all the hours God sends, surely it would be a step towards it if we worked full time. What the system leads to abroad, the scenes of misery there and at home may be left for a further letter. CLIFFORD DIX.

div.head: STUDY Of LANGUAGES.
div.p: THE STUDY Of LANGUAGES.

Sir,—lt is not often that I agree with your correspondent "Clifford Dix," but with his epistle last week I heartily symp ttitiee. There is no doubt at all that if we, as a nation, are to hold our own (not to say, progress), we must wake up. In no matter more than in the study of languages do we need our awakening; and we, if we could possibly get aroused, should again, as of old, surpass "the foreigner." I am glad this subject has been broached at the commence- ment of the winter, as it may lead to some step being taken to increase the educational facilities of the town. There is no town in Lancashire equal in the size of Warrington, so far as I ant aware, where these facilities are less than they are here. Why this should be eel am at a loss to make out. Perhaps it is because we are governed by a stand- still, benighted council, or because the promoters of the ' science classes were discouraged at their failure. But then, everybody is not interested in science. Many have talents in other directions, and to develope these talents no effort has been made for many, many years. The great want— probably the greatest want—of Warrington at the present time is some place where our young men can go and study in the evening. As it is there is no encouragement given to a youth on leaving school to continue his studies. The result is our streets are crowded every night with young men who pass their time smoking cigarettes and annoying girls; and trading thoroughfares resound with the "songs" which proceed from bar parlours where our fast young men are learning habits which will never help them in the race of life. In the study of languages we must do as the foreigners do. "Clifford Dix" points this oat when he in- stances the German youth passing into France and then into England. Now this is precisely where the Englishman fails. He is too—stay-at-home. Instead of going abroad as soon as he can ask his way, he sticks at home, and never gets beyond a certain stage in his study because he has no use for it. But what does the German do I' Why, he often leavea home before be can speak a word of English, finds a friend, say in London, and then begins to study our language. While doing so he turns his hand to anything, and here again the young Englishman fails. But no steady Englishman need turn to anything. All he needs is to save £5O, and then go on the Continent for a year, study the laeguage, get a situation for another year, and then come home. When he does so he will find his £5O will bring him in a return he never could have hoped for before. The matter of cost frightens many young men, but I have repeatedly assured them they need have no fear on this scdre. The cost of living on the Continent (in France or Germany) is just about half of what it is here, and we all know a single young man can get along on £1 a week for board and lodgings. During a fortnight's trip abroad my biggest item was for railway fare, and that, considering the distance I went, was remarkably small. I know a young 'Yankee, who is studying in Germany, who says anybody can live in good style there on 15s a week. My. advice to all young men is go abroad for your holi- days if you cannot go for a longer period, and when there exercise your tongue. Don't be afraid. You will soon find the foreigner trying his English on you, and why not take a leaf out of his book? If you are wrong, he will kindly cor- rect you, as he hopes to profit by speaking English to you. I found foreigners exceedingly alive to the English lan- guage, and directly I was discovered to be an Englishman i they were eager to converse with me. But I saw their I drift, and while instructing got instructed in turn, by reply- 1 in my interrogator's language. It is not mere book learning ' that is wanted ; you must accustom your ear to the spoken language, and to do this imitate the übiquitous German by ' trying at every opportunity the stock of words at your com- mand in any other tongue. If you do you will be delighted at the result. To show the value of foreign languages, I may give an instance from my own knowledge. I had a friend whose lot it was to go and live in an American town, the popula- tion of which was half German. He had every facility to learn German, as he made friends with many Germans (male and female), and was much amongst them. But he 'came away without learning a word, and when he came to England he had not been long in his situation before he was asked if he would like to go to the South-East of &trope, as there was likely to be a vacancy there. This meant that his salary would be instantly trebled, but the first words be uttered were "I cannot speak a foreign language."

div.p: A BOWLING MATCH FOR A COFFIN, OR, A TRIP TO WHITTLE SPRINGS. (From the "B aokbarn Times.") In the" good old times," prior to the introduction of steam tram-cars, which one of our worthy aldermen lately compared to a cottage on wheels, the only method of Blackburn folks getting to. Blackpool, which can be seen from the top of Revidge any clear day, was taking a return ticket by a aping cart, covered with tarpaulin, which took about the same time to come back as a modern locomotive when there is danger on the line at Whitsuntide. For those of this small community (at that time) whose means were limited, by the exercise of the most rigid economy, there was an alternative scheme for getting a day away from home cheap, having a bathe or a bowl, and no fear of any collision en route, and that was a voyage en the Leeds and Liverpool Canal as far as Whittle Springs. Yes, I believe if the files of the Blackburn Times were consulted, some such announcement as the following might be found in the first column of the first page : A Swift Packet will leave the Bottom Lock, Nova Scotia, for Johnson's Hillock (Whittle Springs), on 'Saturday morning at 9 o'clock. Fare, One Shilling. Music and Refreshments on Board." The reader will note that the advertisement contained no nonsense about "weather and other circumstances permitting," such as is seen in reference to the steamer " Winnie," bound from Preston to Lytham, ho, these Wats sailo/ shall I say, weather or not. We encountered no sandbanks on the way; nor did we ever get aground by reason of the treacherous tide. In this respect we had a great advan- tage over unfortunate voyagers down the Ribble. We never had to be hauled ashore in small boats or on men's backs, and have to walk home again, or seek the way to the nearest railway station for succour. The gentleman who chartered the vessel provided no steerage accommo- dation, for we were all cabin passengers, and as the haystacks and farm houses flew, or seemed to fly, ever so swiftly past us, we felt no internal qualms through being rocked in the cradle of the canal: we feared neither fogs, icebergs, nor craft bearing down upon us from the opposite direction. In fact, it was rather slow, but sure. The motive power for these boats was usually supplied , by two bony specimens of the equine tribe ridden by adventurous youths who fancied they were postillions, and whose chief difficulty lay not in restraining the ' natural ardour of the brutes they rode, but in obtaining a speed of five miles an hour out of them, on the average. 1 It was an amusing spectacle to witness the start from 1 the Bottom Lock whilst these two Waterloo chargers 1 were comparatively fresh and eager for the fray. The , rapidity with which we were whirled over aqueducts and , Whizzed under viaducts was at that time considered 4 somewhat dangerous; and, as often happened on the return journey, if some unlucky or tipsy traveller fell off the narrow ledge which did duty as promenade deck i into the canal, then the excitement became feverish. The cry of a "man overboard" roused every passenger 1 to a sense of the danger, and struck with dismay all the 1 females. The young gentlemen who were driving tandem 4 at the end of the tow rope would leap off their fiery un- tamed steeds, the packet would be run ashore, and some 1 of the crew would speedily rescue the dripping one with a boat hook inserted near the heaviest part of his body, and he would be dragged aboard or ashore as circum- stances permitted. On one of these eventful journeys for health and. recreation we were accompanied by two rather remark- able passengers, both well-known townsmen, who . ensconced themselves, when we embarked upon the ' "Happy Jane," within easy reach of the counter where ' Daniel's brew was dispensed by a retired bricklayer who made a Novas "pub" keep him. Both the voyagers had ' red whiskers, and here all other resemblance ceased; for 1 one, whom we will call Jonathan Redhead, was at that time about the same ginth, as the late Chip Billy, of greasy memory, and was descended from the celebrated , Rake of Roddlesworth, and took no particular care ' about his personal appearance; whilst the other, Tom Thorpe, was as careful about the position of each par- ticular hair on his head as the late Michael Manus, once borough treasurer, and that is saying a good deal But he was of a very delicate constitution, and if he drank at all it was only nourishing stout or very dry wines, which he sipped like a canary, in small quantities. Whittle Springs was then in its pomp as an health- resort, for its alkaline spring had been well advertised, and the overflow was used as a bath, so that, ill or well, you could lave in it, drink of it, Sze., ad lib. Here may be seen to this day a first-class oil portrait of J. C. Prince, the reedmaker-poet, who frequented this place perhaps too much for his health like some do Blackpool, and had his admirers from Blackburn and other towns in plenty to treat him. Tom Thorpe had been often to the Springs on a quiet afternoon, for a bowl on the green, but he seldom went by boat, as the company was not select, and the cabin rather stuffy. He was noted for several per- sonal characteristics, which many of your readers will remember. For instance, he always sported a rare flower in his buttonhole, his neatly-fitting trousers were of a yellow tint, his pocket-handkerchief was of the finest cambric, he took snuff on the edge of a sovereign, and it is a fact that he blew his nose every morning at a par- ticular spot in Preston-road, when leisurely strolling down to his office. A late local chronologist, who was of a peering inquisitive nature, noticing a dark ring round his optics one morning, once asked him the meaning of it, when he remarked in his elegant way that he "fell over a cobweb" the night previous. Both these men were supposed to be on their last legs, or, as some say, had one foot in the grave, or, as they say now, Gregory Walker had got his eye on them, and on arriving at Whittle, it being a fine day, their livid i appearance came out n strong relief on the bowling green while they were tossing which should take the )ack in a bowl for drinks. Old Jack Hubberstey, the book hawker, was one of the onlookers, and being in robust health himself had little feeling for anyone else, and he proposed that, as one appeared to be dying of dropsy and the other of diabetes, they should bowl a match of twenty-one up which paid for a good oak coffin, as he said he would not give an old lead spoon for neither of their lives from day today. Jonathan and Tom being in rather better spirits than usual agreed on it at once, and it was settled that in the event of the winner surviving the other he should have his coffin in cash, as it had to cost 50s. The news that a bowling match for an oak coffin was arranged spread all over the grounds at once, and the bath, the spring, the bar, the swings, and the billiard- room were at once deserted to witness the somewhat ghastly game between these two dying men. Jonathan won the toss, and, being so stout, bowled a short length, and Tom won the end by dislodging him, and then took Jonathan from corner to corner' so as to pump out what little breath he had in him. Jonathan came up very slowly with the footer for several ends, amidst the cruel jokes of his associates anent his chances of a cheap wooden suit, but, playing up carefully and patiently, he got the jack when the game stood at nine—love, against him. Jonathan now took Tom on a little daisy bed of his own, and scored rapidly, Tom not being able to get within a yard of the jack, whilst Redhead had touchers nearly every end. This sort of play utterly demoralised Tom, and it was not until the game stood at 19-9, and Jonathan was " up in," that a change took place; for it being only about a twenty yards' length, Tom "struck" and knocked the jack off the green, and the next end got two woods in. He did not let Jonathan get in again until the game stood at 20-19, when Tom, who was a very nervous man, and twisted his body all shapes as he watched his woods run, played wide with his first bowl, and Jonathan played a wood in front, just touching, making the game look like 20 all. Tom's last chance of winning one or two oak planks by throwing his lignum vita in the right direction had now come, and after hesitating a few seconds, he de- cided on trying to shift the jack by going "round-peg." This was a rather risky chance, but it succeeded, for he just shifted the jack about a foot and stopped in. He now counted himself twenty-one, same as Jonathan had done, being "up in," but he was not at liberty to turn the jack, for Jonathan had yet a wood to throw; and Tom had no block to protect his wood from being knocked out. So it came to pass that Jonathan, so fat and scant of breath, with the prospect, if he lost, ot being the first to fill a very big coffin, stood on the "footer" sweating, as some rude men remarked, from fright, with the bowl poised in his hand, undecided whether to play for "a cast" or try to take his oppo- nent out by ' lodging on him." He decided on the last as the only feasible course, and it "came off," for he just gauged the speed of his wood, so that when it struck Tom's it stopped in it's place, and left him with two in, thus winning the coffin by one point. The stakes had not been deposited in the hands of the tenant of Whittle Spring Hotel more than another bowling season before Tom died, and Jonathan went in propria persona to claim the price of his coffin, which he has since carefully deposited in the Death List at the rate of a penny a week, and is living still, reduced to his normal proportions round the waist, and not more than 1601bs. weight the last I saw of him, a standing warning to prophetic people to beware of such habits. I ought to add that these two bowlers disappeared after the match, and they must have come back by the turnpike; but I do not think they walked it—not likely! However they sacrificed their return tickets by the swift packet, and all the fun on the voyage back. The "music on board" consisted of a concertina troubled with chronic bronchitis, which the passengers from Honey Hole called " the band ;" and some volun- teer songsters, whose chief items were" Woodman spare that tree," referring, of course, to the oak tree from which the coffin planks had to be cut; "Ben Bolt," and a nigger song, with a chorus about "He's going where the good niggers go, go, go." Since writing the above I her that Messrs. Troop and Croasdale, coal dealers, have given a trip on the canal to Whittle amongst their friends lately, but whether their swift packet was a coal boat or not was not stated; however, the ancient custom still exists in spite of the competition of "Going-off Clubs" in waggonettes and circular-tour 'buses round Mellor Moor at week- ends, for the hard-worked Blackburn operative will have his jaunts, be they by road, rail, river, or canal. W. HULME.

The twentieth annual meeting of the Trades' Union Congress began on Monday at Swansea,when there was a large attendance of delegates. Among others present were the Mayor of Swansea, Mr. Yeo, M.P., Mr. Broadhurst, M.P., Mr. Cremer, M.P., Mr. W. Crawford, M.P., and Mr. Joseph Arch. The Mayor heartily welcomed the delegates, and hoped their deliberations would advance the well being of the whole community. Mr. Jack, hairman of the Parliamentary Committee, acknowledged the greeting, and, deploring the depression of trade, denied that it was due to the action of free trade. Much of it, he said, was due to foreign State boun- ties and to the iniquitous land laws, which drove thousands of persons into the towns and made the struggle for existence greater. Mr. Bevan, Swan- sea, was elected president ; Mr. Wilkie, Illasgow, vice-president; and Mr. Clarke, Swansea, secretary. Mr. Smythe, London, proposed a resolution con- demning the action of the Government in suppress- ing public meetings in Ireland. Mr. Munro, Belfast, proposed an amendment to the effect that obedience to the law should be enforced as a preliminary to remedying grievances. The amendment was de- feated by 85 to 7; and the resolution was carried by 85 to 1, The delegates were afterwards entertained by the Vayor to luncheon. On Tuesday, upon the reassembling of the Con- gress, the new President, Mr. Bevan, delivered an address. Dealing first with the distress prevailing throughout the country, he said the primary cause was the land being cultivated by too limited a num- ber of people. Other causes were excessive charges by way of royalties, foreign competition, excessive railway rates, foreign bounties, and the false marking of goods by home manufacturers— causes 'which could only be removed by legislation. There were other causes which came within the power of their societies, such as the disorganisation of labour brought about by the improved and exten- sive use of labour-saving machinery, the excessive overtime worked in nearly all trades, and piece- work, which tended to cheapen labour and to the production of an inferior class of goods. The salva- tion of the masses could only be secured by a dis- tinct, robust, and outspoken labour party. He ad- vocated the establishment of international trade congresses, whereby English and foreign werkmen could combine for mutual protection. Their most serious evil he recognised in the unrestrained, un- scrupulous, and remorseless forces of capital. Allud- ing to the eight hours' movement the President said they must make it succeed, and it must be national and apply to all. He would make it a test question at Pirhamentary elections. After a short discussion on the action of Mr. Broadhurst on the eight hours question, the report of the committee was adopted. Discussion followed upon employers' liability, engineers' certificates, factory and work- shop inspectors, and coroners' courts. A somewhat angry discussion followed upon a motion urging upon workmen the imperative necessity of forming labour electoral associations, with a view of return- ing to Parliament, town councils, school boards. and other representative bodies workmen able to speak with authority upon all questions affecting the working classes. The debate on the subject had not concluded when the Congress adjourned. In the evening a large meeting in support of the Inter- national Peace Association was held in connection with the. Congress, and a resolution was passed in favour of referring international differences to arbitration. On Wednesday the discussion of the resolution urging the formation of Labour Electoral Associa- tions was .resumed, and ultimately it was adopted with the addition ot a declaration of opinion in favour of the payment of members. A resolution expressing profound sorrow at the lamentable loss of life at -Exeter on Monday night, and sympathis- ing with the relatives and friends of the deceased and with the injured, was adopted by the Congress, and was at once telegraphed to the Mayor of Exe- ter. Mr. Shipton moved a resolution urging that Parliament should without delay effect such a re- form in the land laws of Great i3ritain as shall re- move all legal enactments that tie up the land beyond the life of one peeson, and thus pave the way for a more general acquirement of the land by the people. The seconder of the motion, Mr. Drum- mond, oi Glasgow, called for the immediate repeal of the game and trespass laws. Mr. Maddison, of Hull, moved an amendment advocating land nation- alisation, to be brought about by the imposition of a land tax on all lands, whether occupied or not. Mr. Joseph Arch contended that the and was in the hands of brigands, and that by releasing it and compelling those Who owned it to cultivate it for the welfare of the people, for whom it was intended, they would be doing a grand work for generations yet unborn. YOUTHFUL Pm:num.—A correspondent says: Soon af- ter dinner on Sunday my attention was called to a large number of young folks who were hurrying towards the pavilion enclosure in the Golborne cricket ground. Has- tening to the spot I found a couple of youths fighting with the ferocity of tigers, and that both were freely using a method of warfare at once dangerous and dastardly--" pur- ring." Youthful partizans were encouraging the combat- ants, and from these I learned that the name of one of the pugilists was "Pee," while the other rejoiced in the sugges- tive, if not euphonious, cognomen of "Bosom." The crowd of onlookers was evidently swayed to excitement, and manifested a lively interest in the progress of the struggle. " Par him i' th' neck" cried one. " (Per him deawn, Besom," exclaimed another, whilst a third, in a most energetic manner, urged upon "Pee "the desirability of "thou-ping Besom's chops." A gentleman who was early on the scene, and who was endeavouring to separate the youthful combatants, was subjected to a storm of abuse from the principals and on-lookers, but undeterred by the cheek, so Characteristic of these precocious youths, he effected a separation. No sooner, however, had this gentle- man left, than hostilities were renewed. Like " Oliver Twist" " I3esom "asked for more, and was quickly accom- modated by his redoubtable opponent. ibeloflizuage born of the strife was terrible in its ferocity and wickedness. The battle was waged with great fury, and ever-changing for- tunes. Now the superior..strength of " Besom " prevailed. anon the greater quickness and agility of " Pee" placed him in the ascendancy. Ultimately a third youth ap- peared, and at once took part in the fray. Copying the example of Sam Weller, in his defence of the person of the immortal Mr. Pickwick, the new comer quickly placed "Pec " hors de combat, and with "one from the shoulder," toppled the other on the top of him. "Pee "ell with his arm underneath him. and "Besom "fell with such force as to break the arm of the former just above the wrist. That such &disgraceful scene should have been enacted on a Sunday afternoon is most discreditable. Legh-street and its environs have earned an unenviable notoriety fork disor- der, and It is high time the strong arm of the law was called into requisition for the purpose of curbing the tur- bulent spirits which have recently been holding high car- nival, and' that unmolested. LONDON. THURSDAY. ' It is not often in political warfare that we find the engineer hoist with his own petard so promptly I and so decisively as the Conservatives have been in I the matter of the Closure. When Mr. Gladstone sub- mitted the proposal, it sought to establish the Closure by a bare majority. The Conservatives, fearful of the application of the rule to themselves, hotly and strenuously objected to this. If they must have the Closure at all,theywoukl like it. on the basis of a two-thirds majority. Finding that impossible, they hit upon the compromise of a minority of 40 and a majority of 200. That, they reckoned, would always keep them clear from the operation of the feared rule. Moreover, it was specially designed to keep in hand the Parnellites, whose numbers at that time did not, for practical purposes, exceed 35. In their selfish and short-sighted policy, they did not take account of the possibility of the Irish repre- sentation being more than doubled, or of the coming of a time when they, being in office, would be fronted and confounded by the very force which in 1882 they encouraged and conspired with to prevent the progress of business under Mr. Gladstone's Gov- ernment. But so it is, and night after night this week, as during the previous fertnight,we have seen the Government, with the powerful engine of the .414S1,ire at their back, impotent to control a cora- -IParatively small minority in the House of Commons. For some time we have heard nothing of the famous "National Party," with the creatien and establishment of which Mr. Chamberlain was wont to threaten the regular Liberal party. It was found upon going further into the matter that the party would consist of Mr. Jesse Collings, together with Mr. Chamberlain's cob nections by blood or mar- I rage, 411 told, the "National party" at its incep- toff Consisted of sonis five persons. That is, of b our se , no reason why the party should not have been successfhlly established. Mahomet founded his far reaching empire with less than five to begin With, and Morraomsm at the outset had no more adherents. A distinctive and hopeless feature about the "National party" is that the would-be founder and the original group of recruits have themselves lost heart, and we hear nothing more of "the party." On the other hand Liberalism, under the leadership of Mr. Gladstone, is steadily recovering its strength. The soberest members of the inner circle of the party organisation are at length declar- ing their opinion that a general election may now be faced with fair certainty of success. The prin- cipal difficulty in the way is the tenacity of Ministers. They have a Parliamentary majority, which, whatever happens in the country, keeps them secure in their seats. It will take a \ long tie, even at the pace recently achieved, to change this majority into a minority. In the meantime, the country will be governed by a set of men who notoriously do not possess its confidence. This should make electors careful next time they get a chance. Some months ago, whilst Dissentient Liberalism was in a much more flourishing condition than it is at present, a proposition was made at the Reform Club for a subscription to give a commission for the portrait ot Lord Hartington to be set up in the club where Mr. Gladstone, Mr. Bright, and Mr. Villiers already look down from the walls. The suggestion was not adopted without considerable hesitation. It was felt that it would be a considerable blow to the so-called Liberal Unionists if, having started the project, it fell through for lack of subscribers. But everything lociked so bright for the Dissentients, and the Reform Club being a pretty strong centre for their community, it was determined to adven- ture it. The subscription was limited to a guinea each, a subscription book was laid on the table in the reading-room, and there was a diligent looking up of anti-Gladstonians. The result has, however, not been very successful. There was a considerable influx at first, but of late the procession of sub- scribers has sorely lagged. The growing im- pression appears to be that if any club in Pall Mall is to be honoured by having the portrait of Lord Hartington hung on its walls, it should be the Carlton, whither it is believed Lord Hartington is rapidly tending. The club is now closed for re- pairs, but I hear that the total number of sub- scribers does not exceed 320. This, of course, falls far short of the requirements. The principal por- trait painters of the day get .E.BOO and .£l,OOO for a portrait. The latter is Mr. Roll's charge. As things go now in the depressed state of art, .£5OO for a portrait would command the services of only a second rate artist. Mr. Bright's was the last por- trait which the Reform Club acquired by subscrip- tion, and £6OO was put down in less time than it has taken to collect a little over half that sum to do honour to Lord Hartington. Lord Hartington very rarely visits the Reform Club, and when he looks in does not often penetrate farther than the great hall. He is, indeed, not a clubable man, and the more secluded precincts of Brooks's meets his necessities. Mr. Bright is, when in town, almost a daily visitor at the Reform. He reads the papers there and lunches (a meal which he calls dinner) and takes his tea. lam told by an old member that it is quite a common sight to see the former Liberal chief seated in the smoke-room with a semi-circle of members gathered round him listening to his violent denunciation of Mr. Glad- stone. It is, my friend tells me, quite shocking to hear the gratuitous abuse he levels at his former colleague who never speaks Of him without respect, and never alludes to his political position except in tones of regret that after so long stepping the Liberal highway together their ways should have parted. Talking about portraits, a curious, thing hap- pened the other day. A former member of the House of Commons, ousted at the last General Elec- tion, and a little sick of London, decided to sell his house and furniture in Portland-place. Amongst his possessions were two small miniatures, one of Mr. Gladstone and one of Mr. Bright. These were included in the sale, and the ex-member had some curiosity to see which would bring the larger sum. He mentioned the forthcoming sale to Mr. Bright, and promised to let him know the result. The auc- tioneer, with that lordly contempt of small things, sold the miniatures in a single lot, which brought 30s, not quite the value of the frames, the late possessor says. To this low value do our great men come-at last ! But even this is better than the fate of Lord Beaconsfield. It was recently stated dur- ing the hearing of a case in the Edinburgh Court of Sessions that certain portraits of Lord Beacons- field were sold by weight. Some time ago, when. the "Freeman's Journal" was floated as a limited company, I mentioned a House of Commons report that Mr. Dwyer Gray, in . allotting the shares, had been very kind to his col- leagues of the Home Rule party. As the shares went at once to a considerable premium, anyone who got an allotment simply had a present in gold. I have just seen the original rol/rof share-

OUR FINANCIAL LETTER. LFROM OUR OWN CORRESPONDENT.] 23, Old Broad-street, E.C. The Stock Exchange showed unwonted activity euring the earlier part of the week. This was due to the activity of the American market which exhibited a sharp rise all round. In fact the brokers were beginning to assume a most business-like air and the one reply In calling upon them began to assert itself "can't see you now, am very busy." What had happened was the inquiry, to which came the answer " haven'tyou heard of boom in American." Unfortunately the so called boom was not to last long. By Wednesday the bubble had burst, and prices came tumbling down as fast, if not faster, than they had gone up, so little real steadiness is there in the market at tte present time, and until the general public come in there is not likely to he any real firmness, as without the support of the public the markets can have no solidity. There is very little doubt, as was pointed out in these columns a short time since, it is from America where the first manifestations of improved business must come, and al- though the present spirit has been rather short lived, it is sure to return very soon and obtain solid support from the outside. Hudson Bay shares, to which attention was called a week or two ago, have shown a further steady rise, and have not been affected by the fall of other securities, the rise being steady and gradual, and Lose who took advantage of the advice must have cause to congratulate themselves. A preliminary contract has been executed between the Baltimore and Ohio Railroad and Messrs. J. S. Morgan and Co., Baring Brothers and Co., and Brown, Shipley, sad Co., of London, and their allied houses on this side. The con- tract provides for the negotiation of £5.000,000 of Baltimore and Ohio consolidated s's, and £5,000,000 of Baltimore and Ohio preferred stock, for the purpose of paying of the en- tire floating debt of the company, and placing it on a sound inancial basis. 1 Among the conditions are that the management of the I, company shall be placed in competent hands satisfactory to I the syndicate. The syndicate is composed of the houses I mentioned above, together with Mesars. Drexel, Morgan, and Co.. Drexel and Co., Brown Brothers and Co. and Kidder. Peabody, and Co. It la announced that on September 15th the Commercial Cable Co. will reduce its cable rates to 12 per cent a word Ito Great Britain, Ireland, and France. and 15 cents a word Ito Germany. It is also stated that the company has in- creased Its capital stock by £2,000,000, making the total of £6,000,000 in order to pay for the recent extension of the cable to Waterville, in Ireland, and Bristol, in Englaod, and for other new plant.

Mr. Blake, who has since retired on his competency, had 15 ordinary shares and 50 preference. Mr. Chance had 25 ordinary shares. while Hr. Clancey was content with 10. Mr. Crilly had 20 ordinary and 10 preference. Mr. Flynn had 25 ordinary, and Mr. T. P. Gill 50 ordinary, which he would find more profitable than his letters to the'" New York Tribune.' Mr. Harrington bagged 60 ordinary shares and 15 preference, whilst Tim Healy was satisfied with 50 shares, and his brother Mau- -rice with 25. Dr. Kenny. bad 100 shares, Mr. Leahy 75, Justin McCarthy 50, and his -son Huntley 25. T. P. O'Connor went in for 100-shares, whilst Mr. Parnell had not less than 400, Mr. Sex- ton taking 100. Others with less familiar names had allotments in proportion. The luckiest man is a priest man Daniel, who got not less than 1,150 shares, premium on which would come to a pretty sum. Mr. Devitt had 200 shares. Bishops and archbishops were highly favoured. Dr. Croke had 1500 shares, the Archbishop of Cashel 200, the Archbishop of Dublin 200. and Dr. Walsh 500. It is a long time since lrish patriots had such a wind- fall. We are not likely to see a real Life of Lord Beaconsfield. Lord Rowton, to whom the work and the materials for it were bequeathed, finds it too much for him ,and has abandoned the task. It was I a curious choice for a man of Lord Beaconsfield's Idiscrimination to select his secretary for the work. Lord Rowton has never displayed any literary ability, has never as far as I know attempted any litei ary work. I gathered in conversation with him shortly after Lord Beaconsfield's death that he was appalled by the enormity of the task. Lord Beaconsfield kept every important or interesting letter addressed to him; but this he achieved by the simple practice of throwing them into a large open box. When it was filled to its utmost, the box was locked up and another, taken. It would have been the work of nearly a lifetime to deal with this heterogenous mass, and Lord Rowton after hanging hesitatingly round for some years, has found relief in the conviction that the correspondence is of t2o delicate a nature to be published in this cen- tury.

INDIAN FINANCE-On the motion for going into com- mittee on East India Revenue, Mr. BRADLAUGH regretted that the only occasion afforded the House for considering the wishes and grievances of the natives of India should be postponed until so late a period of the session as to to pre- vent a fair consideration of such wishes and grievances. He insisted that it was not by new military domination that we should look forward to the maintenance of our , In- dian rule, and referred to a variety of matters in which re- form in the system of government was necessary, if we were to secure the good will of the people. -- Dwain ow A Otani:mutes WIFE.—Mrs. Flaherty, tf Cthe Rev. W. Flaherty, the esteemed incumbent of hoflwoninity Church, Parr Mount, died somewhat suddenly oiofineday. The deceased lady, who had gained the love rT M poorer portion of the parishioners by her many acts yoffehristian charity, had been for some years in failing health, but the end came with painful suddenness. The greatest ;sympathy is felt for the rev, gentleman and the family in their bereavement. The funeral was arranged for to-day (Friday). DISGRACErM CONDUCT A LENIENT SENTENCE.— Before Alderman J. Harrison and Mr. A. Sinclair, at the Town Hall, on Saturday, James Fildes, a cripple, who lodged in Water-strec:, was charged in custody with inde- cent behaviour towards a little girl nine years of age. By the offer of a halfpenny the prisoner induced the girl to enter a yard off the Victoria passage for an immoral pur- pose. Chief-constable Wood said the prisoner had been many times before the magistrates, including one committal of six months for an indecent assault. He was a very bad character, and a nuisance to the town.—The Bench corn. mitted the prisoner for two months.

As to the Rubs, Mines, he did not think there were grounds for complaint, as no lease bad been en• tared into with Mr. Streder, and none would be granted until the value of the mines was ascertained. After observations from Mr. R. T. Reid, Sir J. Goan' proceeded to make the annual statement of the condition of Indian finance which he said was not very prosperous. The accounts showed an improvement in net Indian revenue, but the net expen- diture had increased owing to additional military charges, and the result WAS that the prospects for 1877-8 were worse than when the estimates were framed. Instead of there being a surpfus of £113,700 there was a deficit of £593,000 ler the ensumg year. He concluded by proposing the usual resolution confirming the accounts. LYNN. OUGHTRINGTON FOOTBALL CLUB.—On Tuesday last, A 4 general meetmg of the Oaghtrington, Park Asso,ffation Foothill Club was held, at which Mr U 0 Smith was re- ' elected captain of the first team, and Mr W Gosling sub- ' captain. Mr II Everton, junior, was also re-elected secre- tary. WESLEYAN BAND or Hop.—On Tuesday evening, a meeting of this Bind of Hope was held in the Wesleyan school. The following officers were elected :—President. Mr F 0 Mouton; vice-president, Mr Brown; secretary, Mr John Harrington. A cordial vote of thanks was passed to Mr rhOtTIAS Ashton for his long and valued services as president, he having held that office for 30 years. SERIOUS INJURIES TO & WOREWAN.—On Tuesday, a labourer named Thomas Drtnkwater, who is employed by the Local Board, met with an accident of a somewhat serious character. Under the superintend nce of the surveyor (Mr. Mort) several men were employed in putting up a ventilator on Eagle Brow. The shaft of the ventilator was to run up a tree on the plantation in the occupition of Captain Ban• ning, and it was while lopping off some branches that Drinkwater accidentally cut the branch by which he was steadying himself on a ladder. He in consequence fell a distance of about 18 fe-t, with the result that his right Thigh was fractured and his left shoulder dislocated. As a doctor could not be found immediately, the injured limbs were bound up under the superintendence of the Rev. Mr. Rogerson, and later on Drinkwater was conveyed to the infirmary at Warrington by the direction of D. Bra- bazon. WEDDING AT 00GHTRI1(GTON.—The wedding Of Mr. Wil- liam Critchley, ciptain of the ship Glen Otani., to Miss Miry Ellen Gibbon, of the Higher-lane, took place on Sat- urday last, at two p.m., in Oughtrington Church. The Rey. Joseph C alien, M.A., of Canterbury, late rector of this parish, officiated. The bride wore a dress fashionably made of heliotrope colour, and a white bonnet trimmed with white lace. She was given away by her uncle, Mr. Richardson, of Edinburgh. Miss Cameron was first bridesmaid, followed by Miss Critchley and Miss Emily Richardson. Mr. Critch- iey's best man was Mr. Morris, of Southport. The bride re- ceived a very valuable list of presents from bar various friends, she being very highly respected. In the evening the newly-married pair left for Fleetwood. where Captain Critchley's ship is now lying. Before the ceremony Mr. 0. G. Smith, organist of St. Peter's. played Andante in A (Smart) and Offertoire in D (Batisle), and at its conclusion Mendelssohn's Vi'edding March.

COLLISION ON THE MERSEY. A collision, resulting in the sinking of the brigantine Constance. occurred in the Mereey on Thursday morning, although it fortunately happened that the crew of seven men succeeded in making good their escape. It appears that the Isle of Man steamer Mena's Isle was lying in the river, near the Sloyne. about six o'clock on Thursday morning, as the tide was running out strongly. The steamer was at anchor. The Constance, a brigantine, was coming down the river with a cargo of salt from Runcorn, which she was conveying to the Tyne, when she was carried by the strong current right across the bows of the steamer. The crew made all efforts to clear the Mona's Isle, but the tide was too strong. The impact was very heavy, the bri- gantine receiving such damage that she at once commenced to sink. She was under the charge of Captain Langlois, and he and the remainder of the crew—seven hands in all— succeeded in getting away in their own boat before their vessel went down. The cable of the Mona's Isle, although heavily struck, still held, and the brigantine literally elided down it until she reached the bed of the river. It is stated that the Conhtance sank immediately on top of the anchor of the Mona's Isle, in which C4BO it will be necessary to slip the steamer's cable before she can get away from the spot. The Mona's Isle does not appear to have been much, if any, damaged, and the collision is not likely to interfere with her sailing. The shipwrecked men made for the pier. head, where they landed, and subsequently went to the local Sailors' Home, where they were received by the su- perintendent, Mr. Thomas Hanmer. The Constance be- longs to Messrs Bellingham and Company, of Jersey, and was a vessel of about 300 tons gross register. At low water her masts could be seen a good distance above the surface of the water.

RUNCORN BOARD OF COMMISSIONERS. The first meeting cf this Board since the election was held on Thursday at the Town Hall, Waterloo-road. Mr. Dobson presided, and there were present —Messrs. Grico, Hatikinson, Smith, White, Fisher, Lightburn, Whittaker, Taylor, Linaker (law clerk), Marshall (secretary), Barker (surveyor.) APPOINTMENT OF COMMITTEES —The following com- mittees were appointed :_Canal Boats and General Pur- poses : Messrs. Grice, Taylor, Whittaker, White, Mellor, Elaukinson, Smith.—Highway and Buildings: The whole of the members of the Board.—Finance : Messrs. Fisher, Meadowcroft, Pritchard, Liaison, Taylor. Grice, Speakman, Lightburn .—Parliamentary and Legal::—Messrs. Fisher, Meadowcroft, Taylor, Lightburn, am: Speakman.— Health : Messrs Lightburn. Lake, Taylor, Grice, Piitchard, Hankinson, and Smith.— Waterloo Bridge : Messrs Pritch- ard, White, Taylor, Lake, Fisher, and Timmins —Library Committee : Messrs Lake, Moss, Wood, W Handley, Ma- wood, Frith, Norman, Riley, Imison, the chairman of the Commissioners, and Elankinson.—During the course of the proceedings, Mr Smith inquired how it was Mr Shaw's name did not appear on any of the committees.—The Chairman replied that Mr. Shaw was about to leave the town, and would not then be a member of the Board. RETURNING OFFICERS' EXPENSES.—The Chairman an- nounced his expenses as returning officer amounted to £8 103 641.—Mr. Hankinson moved that a cheque be drawn for the amount —Mr. Grice seconded the proposition, and re- marked that on the day of the election he met with a gentle- man who had been returning officer at another town. That gentleman expressed his surprise at the small amount of the returning officer's expenses at Runcorn. lie remembered one time when at the place with which he was connected the sum 0 £BO was spent. He (Mr. Grice) thought the
ratepayers of Runcorn might congratulate themselves that they were in the bands of a body of men that were very chary of expenses, and wanted to keep them down.—The motion was carried. . .

THE WIDNES INTER-WORKS • RUGBY FOOTBALL COMPETITION: SECOND ROUND. HvramesoN's V. GOSSAGE'S. A further stage in the toter-Works Football Competition at Widnes was reached on Monday evening, when the first match of the second round, between teams from the works of Messrs. John Hut- chinson and Co. and Messrs. W. Gossage and Sons, took place on the Whines Football Ground, Lowerhouse-'ane. 'there was a capital gate, and a good game was witnessed. The superiority of the soap men over their opponents, how- ever, was soon manifest, and but for the good defensive play of Hutchinson's team, who were somewhat heavily handicapped in Mr. J. H. Smith, their captain, not being able to play in consequence of an accident received in the first round, the score would have been considerably more than it was. Except in the second half, when playing with the wind. Hutchinson's men were never able to get near their opponents' lines, and the game, which was a forward One threughout, ultimately re ulted in a win for Messrs. Gossage's by three tries, scored by Pennington, Bingham, and Burgess, and twelve minor points, to Hutchinson's two minors. The teams were :imilar to what they were in the first round. UAsKELL, DEACON AND Co.'s V. BROCK ANTI Bi7LLI- VAN'S.—the trial ef strength between these team* bad been looked forward to with considerable interest, inasmuch as both contained amongst them players of merit, and neither had played in the first round, Deacon's having a walk over and Sullivan's having a bye. There was, therefore, a large number of persons on the ground, and their surmises as to the toughness of the struggle were not unfounded, for a better and more tightly contested game has not taken place during the whole competition. In the first half Deacon's men scored three minors in quick succession, and then Cook got over for Brook's from a pass by Boyle. The kick at goal by Barker failed. A minor point, accredited to Deacon's just before call of time, was the only other point scored, the intervening play loose forward being most exciting, the ball travelling rapidly forward and backward from one end of the field to the other. The gems, therefore, resulted in a draw, four points each, and will have to be played once again. It is probable, however that on the n'qct occasion Deacon's will come out the winners as two of their best men. Williams and Gallimore, were away on Thursday. The following were the teams : Gaskell, Deacon, and Co.: Full back, Brannon; threequarter backs, • J. Smith, Johnson, Burgess, and Charles; half-backs. Mc- Gurn!' and Gleave : forwards. Fogg (captain), Smart, Hoole, Lyons, Cosgrove, F. Wright, Textan, and Rooney; umpire, t Mr. W. Riddle. Brock and Sullivan's: Fall back, J. Min- . ton; threequarter backe' Wright, Barker (captain). and . Abraham!; half backs, Bradshaw and Atherton ; forwards, Meagher, Flynn, Bowles, Clare, Shuttleworth, Houghton, Cook, Boyle, and Sauce; umpire, Mr. J. Brown; referee Mr. Lewis. St. Helens.

REV. PETER McKENZIE AT WIDNES. With the object of increasing the funds of the Widnes Wesleyan Circuit, the Rev. Peter McKenzie. the celebrated lecterer on religious subjects, paid a visit to Wldnea. In the afternoon, at the Victoria-road Chapel, he preached a powerful service to a congregation of fair proportions, many friends from the surrounding towns being present. For the convenience of those present tea was subsequently I served in the schoolroom, and about 120 •persons sat down at the tables. In the evening the sacred building was well filled with an audience assembled to hear Mr. McKenzie lecture on" Saul, the first King of Israel, a man who missed his mark." Mr. ri. Wade Deleon, J.P.. bad been an- nounced to preside, but he was suffering from an affection or the throat, and Dr. Cameron had forbidden him to go out at night, or to address a public meeting. The audience, through Mr. T. S. Swale, expressed sympathy with Mr. Deacon in his illness. The chair Was taken by Mr. W. Newell, of Garsloo, who was supported by the Rev. R. Burdon, Rey. J. Bryant, Rev. G. W 974 (BencOrn), andM MIS S. Robinson and T. S. Swale. The lecturer Said the history of Saul was like an inspired tragedy, aid poets and musicians had clothed it with a fas- cination and genius, and with the spell of romance. He pointed out that the Israelltish government was a theoc- racy, and for 450 years after entering into Canaan this kind of government continued until the people had a longing te have a king to rule over them, like the rest of the nations round about them. The lecturer gave a characteristic ac- count of the selection of Saul as king, describing him as standing in the midst of the people like a Methodist preacher at a tea meeting at the top of a form. (Laugh- ter.) But there were always some people discontented, and a few of the Israelites asked " What can that daddy long legs do. (Laughter.) They tell me he is a good hand at hunting strays ; and he looks like it. Why doesn't he stop at it 2' (Laug'..ter.) In the first year of his reign Saul exercised benevolence, modesty, and heroism, but the in- fluence of power upon the mind of a monarch was seen in his later arbitrary and cruel conduct, and his rebellion against God. A graphic relation of his futile attempts against the life of David was given, and how, setting him- self against the Lord. he visited the dark and diabolical den of the Witch of Ender, to seek her aid. Next i'ay he was slain in the battle against the Philistines. His life failed because he set his heart against Gad, and the lesson to be I learned from it was the importance of personal piety. Without personal piety all the honours and emoluments would come short of the mark, for without personal piety we had no 'security against the enormities of criminality. (Applause.) On the proposition of Mr. Swale, seconded by Mr. S. Robinson, a cordial vote of thanks was passed to Mr. McKenzie. In replying, the Lecturer said he had conducted about 500 services this year, and travelled perhaps 10,000 miles, but he could make a fair show in the flesh yet. (Laughter). He promised to pay a visit to Widnes next year. A vote of thanks to the Chairman concluded the 'meet- ing.

WIDNES FREE PUBLIC LIBRARY. The monthly meeting was held at the Town Hall yes- terday. Mr. H. Wade Deacon presided, and there were:pre- sent r. O'Keeffe, Messrs S Sadler, J Midwood, W Sadler, I+ 11 Pankhurst, and J T Allen (clerk to the Local Board). Lraaanten's REPORT.—The Librarian's report stated that during August there were borrowed from the lending department and read and consulted in the reference depart- ment 4,273 volumes, being for the lending department an iocrease of 812,and for the reference department a decrease of 21. The number of guarantee forms received during the same period was 168, for which cards had been issued. The cash received for fines, damage to books, dm., amounted to £2 17a BJ. The total daily attendances at the reading room was 11,921, and the average daily attendance 441. PROPOSED FREE LECTITRES.—Mr. Allen said that at the List meeting he was instructed to get some information with regard to free lectures in connection with free libraries. He had received a letter from Mr. Altree, clerk to the manor of Aston Local Board, Birmingham, who said as regarded the illegality of defraying the costs' incurred out of the penny rate, the Aston Local Board considered the Public Libraries Act gave authority under section 21, which said the council, board, or committee may' provide certainl things for the use of the library or museum or school, and may make regulations for the use of the libraries, museums,l schools, and for the admission of the public. The Aston Local Board regarded these lectures as scholastic, and there- fore covered by the above provision and the Local Govern- ment Board auditor, who audited the accounts, adopted this view.—Mr. Robert K. Dent, the librarian, who is secretary to the Free Lecture movement, gave a few notes with re- gard to the working of the free libraries at Aston. The ex- penses under this head, he said, were limited by the Com- mittee to £1.5 per annum. and as they paid no fees to lec- turers this amply covered the expenses incurred. Out of this they had to pay for the hire of a room, the travelling expenses of lecturers, printing, &c. Mr. Dent added that the Widnes committee would probably find in their own neighbourhood a number of men thoroughly able and will- ing to give lectures, and by the payment of railway fares they might often get a man of repute from some neighbour- ing town to give a lecture freely.—A programme of ltdt season's lectures was enclosed, and the Chairman remarked that it WAS a very good one.—The Clerk read the complete clause referred tomn the letter, and the Chairman remarked that it appeared that the committee had the power to organise free lectures and defray the expenses. Re sug- gested that a committee of three gentlemen should be formed to consider the matter.—On the proposition of Mr. Pankhurst, seconded by Mr. S. Sadler, the Chairman, Dr. O'Keeffe, and Mr. Midwood were appointed the com- mittee.

PARTINGTOII.—Sunday last was the day on which the Congregationalists of Partington held their chapel and school anniversary. In the afternoon there was a service of song entitled "Whiter than snow," given by an augmented choir, under the leadership of Mr. Hazelhurst. Mr. Whitfield, presi- ded at the organ, and Mr. E. B. Scott was thereader. i The sermon n the evening was preached by the Rev. J. H. Gaston, of Iymm, to an over- flowing audience, the collections amounting to £8 lOs Bd. SUCCESS OF A SCHOOL OF ABM STUDENT. —We are pleased to see that Mr. W. G. Knight, of Nant- wich, and student of the Warrington School of Art, has been awarded a National Art scholarship by the Science and Art Department, South Kensington. The value of the scholarship to commence with is £52 a year, whilst it is possible for this sum to be increased to £lO4 a year. The number of candi- dates from the various schools of art throughout the United Kingdom competing for these scholar- ships is invariably largely in excess of the small number at the disposal of the examiners. The com- petition is, therefore, very keen, and Mr.. Knight must be congratulated on his brilliant success. • WARRINGTON. THE LANCASHIRE MAGISTRACY.— The roll of Justices of the Peace for the county palatine of Lancashire has just been issued. It shows that there are 731 gentlemen and noblemen upon the Commission of the Peace. Sir Gilbert Greenall, M.P., Walton Hall, Warrington, and Mr. Henry Stan- ton, Warrington, who qualified on the 12th of January, 1843, bead the West Derby Hundred list. THE WRATH/IR.—The long continued drought has been broken by a considerable downfall of rain since the commencement of the present .month. The rainf..ll, which has been extremely slight during the months of Jaly and August, having only amounted during that time to iv inches, has amounted to 211 inches since the Ist September. This has been accompanied by a lowering of the temperature, the mean temperature being 56 F. during the first week of September, compared with 61.4 the mean of the same period of 1886. A LOCAL CENTENARIAN.—Mrs. Ann Birch, an old lady who lives at Town's-end, has recently celebra- ted her 100th birthday. She buried her husband nearly half a century ago, and has lived in War- rington all her life. A member of our staff called to see her on Tuesday, and ascertained that although she has reached such a ripe old age, she yet enjoys excellent health, and is able to walk, though but slowly. She has good eye- sight, and her hearing is not much affected. Asked if she was in the habit of smoking, she admitted the impeachment, and also expressed her partiality tor an occasional_pinch of snuff. WARRINGTON PARISH CHURCH SUNDAY SCHOOL. —The Young Men's Bible Class and a few friends in connection with the Sunday school had a trip to Manchester Exhibition by road on Saturday. The conveyances, three in number, started from the National School at 8-0 o'clock a.m. The day turned out fine, and the excursionists had a nice drive through Lymm, Bowdon, &c. (making a short stay at Dunham Massey to be photographed), and reach- ing Manchester about 11-0. At the Exhibition the pictures and fairy fountain came in for a good share of attention. The excursionists arrived home safely, having had a long and enjoyable out. STRIKE AT COCKFIEDGE FACTORY.—On Monday morning a strike of a somewhat novel character, and which was not of long duration, took place among the girls employed in several of the carding- rooms of Cockhedge Factory. It appears that the old overseer of the department had been removed and a new one put in his place, and at this the female employes took offence and "struck." Later on in the day they made a public display of their i feelings by walking some of the streets n proces- sion, but they were ultimately dispersed by the rain. The" strike," however, came to an end on Tuesday morning, when those who had "'come out" on the previous day went back to the factory, and were. after some_delay, re-admitted. BIRTH IN THE STREETS. On Sunday morning about six o'clock, a married woman named Ellen Matthews was taken suddenly ill on Warrington Bridge, near the drinking fountain. The constable on the beat quickly had his attention called to the matter, and steps were taken for the poor woman's relief. While P.C. Bracewell went in search of proper assistance, P.C. Corbett ran to Mr. Connor's establishment in Sankey-street, for a cab, and Ser- geant Shaw went to the house of Mr. John Monks, publican, for some brandy. By the time the mid- Wife, Mrs Locker, arrived, a fine female child was born. Both mother and child were at once wrapped in some clothing provided by Mrs Locker, and they 'were conveyed to the hospital at the Workhouse, where proper attention was given to them. Mrs Matthews, it appears, belongs to Runcorn, and had walked from that town during Saturday night as she had heard that her husband, whom she had not seen for some time, was working in Trar- rington. HARVEST FESTIVAL A.T GREAT SANlKEY.—Harvest thanksgiving services were held on Sunday. at Sankey Parish Church. The ini:erior of the edifice was as usual tastefully decorated with seasonable products. In the morning the sermon was preached by the Rev. B. B, Prescott, and in the evening by the Rev. T. Chambers, rector of Hale. There was a large congregation at each service, and particularly in the evening. In the course of his sermon, Mr. Chambers referred to the abundant harvest with which the country was this year blessed, not a drop of rain having fallen during the ingathering of the wheat and hay crops, and as no harvest service was complete without a ' thankoffering, he asked them -ror their aid in completing the new schools in con- nection with the church. He was told that there was still a debt approaching £3OO, connected with the building, and he asked his hearers to assist in wiping that debt out. Up to the present they had helped their vicar in all the good works which he had initiated, and he was certain they would assist him in bringing this work to a satisfactory con- clusion also. Last year he remembered asking them for their aid in completing the gallery of the church, and now heobserved that it was filled with people. If ever there was a -time in our history when Sunday school teaching was necessary it was the present ; and, therefore, the completion of their schools was an urgent necessity. The offertory at both morning and evening services was in aid of the new Sunday schocls. Suitable hymns were sung, Miss Standish presiding at the organ. LORD WINMARLEIGH AT GARSTING SHOW. The annual agricultural show at Garstang was held on Thursday. There was a ;very good show in all classes. At one o'clock a dinner was held in the show yard, Mr. W. J. Fitzherbert-Broekholes, -the president of the society, in the chair. Lord Win- marleigh, who received a cordial greeting, proposed "Success to the Garstang and District Agricultural Society." He said that while the county society, which had recently held its meeting at Manchester, was doing great service to Lancashire and the ad- joining districts over which its operations extended, such societies as that in whose interest they were then assembled were doing equally good service to the tenant farmers residing within their areas. He was sorry he could not congratulate them upon the present state of the agricultural interest. He -wished he could, but it so unfortunately happened that at the present moment not only was there a depression in prices, but several other circum- stances had militated against them. He 'need niot allude to the weather, which had interfered with the getting in of the crops, or to the severe frost which a few weeks ago cut down their potatoes. The general conditions of agriculture were not nearly so prosperous as at that time last year. Notwithstanding, he believed that those meetings were of advantage, and that they contributed towards the bringing together of landlords and tenants. If ever there was a time when it was de- sirable that landlords and tenants should be on friendly terms and come to an understanding_ the one with the other, it was the present. (Hear, hear.) They found themselves confronted by many difficulties, and they none of them knew exactly how to proceed. Speaking to them as one of the landlords of North Lancashire, he could simply ex- press to them his desire to meet the difficulties of the present season in the best and most honourable manner he could. (Applause.) WitweXii To THE NEW WESLEYAN liinnemus. —On Thursday evening the ministers recently ap- pointed to the Warrington Wesleyan Circuit—the Revs. W. Brookes and E. H. Jackson, who succeed the Revs. J. R. AMOS and G. E. Cutting—were wel- comed by the members of the congregation at a tea and meeting held in Bold-street Wesleyan Chapel. About 150 persons sat down to tea, and at the subse- quent meeting the chair was occupied by the super- intendent of the circeit, the Rev. G. E. Young, who was supported on the platform by the Revs. W. Brookes and E. H. Jackson and other gentlemen.— The Chairman, in the course, of an address, heartily bade the new preachers welcome. They very much regretted the removal to other circuits of the Revs. J. H. Jones and G. E. Cutting, but it was a satisfaction to know that they would be succeeded by two such capable men as the Revs. W. Brookes and E. H. Jackson—(hear, hear,)—who came to Warrington with a firkt-class reputation. There was a great deal of work to be done in Warrington. Re should like;to make the two chief centres of the circuit Bolestreet and Bewsey-road— exceed- ingly strong. There was also Sankey Bridges. where the cause was flourishing, Penketh, where they were getting on fairly well, Padgate, which might soon be the head of a circuit, Lymm, where there should be a resident minister. Then there was Appleton and Antrobus, Whitley and Hatton, and last, but not least. Moore. He hoped that they should see a revival in these vil- lages soon.—Mr. Silcock (circuit steward), then read letters explaining inability to attend from Messrs. Dodds, R. Cook, Hayward, E. J. Guest, Garnett, and Richardson. He also cordially wel- coraed the new preachers.—Mr. E. Brown, Lymm, in the course of a few remarks, said he hoped that at Lymm they would soon have a resident minister, and on behalf of Lymm he also welcomed Mr. Brookes and Mr. Jackson.—Short speeches were also given by Messrs. John Bennett, William Ben- nett (Padgate), E. Lawton, Knowles (Appleton), Isaacs, Stringer, and E. Ford, and brief replies were made by the Rev. W. Brookes and the Rev. ; E. H. Jackson.
